C.2
Observation-Based Stickiness

We allow a stickiness function to depend on what nature observes,
i.e.
, its private observations
Z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}}
, public observations
Z_{\circ}
, and the agent’s actions
A
.
To define such stickiness functions, we denote for each variable
v\in U
the state-action pairs it influences by
v^{s,a}\colon S\times A\to\{0,1\}
.

An example of an observation-based stickiness function is:

\displaystyle\forall v\in U,z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet}\in Z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},z_{\circ}\in Z_{\circ},a\in A.

\displaystyle\quad\mathsf{stick}(v,z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a)=1\iff\exists s\in S.O^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet}(s)=z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet}\land O_{\circ}(s)=z_{\circ}\land v^{s,a}(s,a)=1.

Under observation-based stickiness, a variable only sticks if there is a possibility that it influenced the actual transition based on the last observations and actions.
This means that all variables that influence both a state with observations
z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}
and the chosen action
a
stick.
The intuition behind observation-based stickiness is that nature only needs to optimize for the transitions it might influence at that given point in time.
Note that this stickiness does not take the entire history into account, so there can still be restrictions on variables that nature knows cannot influence the actual transition, as can be seen in the discussion of the right example below.

Appendix D
Uncertainty Assumptions Matter

In this appendix, we elaborate on the results established in
Theorem

1
and its proof.
See
1

In the following four subsections, we compare tuples of R(PO)MDPs which only differ in either the stickiness or the order of play.
The first two subsections focus on differences in the stickiness, and the latter two focus on differences in the order of play:

1.

Full stickiness versus zero stickiness in an
(s,a)
-rectangular model (
Section

D.1
).

2.

Full stickiness versus observation-based stickiness versus zero stickiness in an
a
-rectangular model (
Section

D.2
).

3.

Agent first versus nature first in a simple model (
Section

D.3
).

4.

Agent first versus nature first in an
a
-rectangular full sticky model (
Section

D.4
).

For each of the tuples of RPOMDPs, we first state the value functions given agent and nature policies.
In principle, we use the sets of mixed nature policies
\Theta^{{mix}}
for computing the optimal value and policy, which are equivalent to the original sets of stochastic policies, as shown in
Section

G.3
.
However, in three of the four RPOMDP tuples, we can consider deterministic nature policies instead of mixed nature policies, as discussed in more detail in
Section

D.1
.
For legibility reasons, we switch back to the stochastic policy notation when writing the optimal policy.

Given the value functions and the types of optimal policies, we used the 3D calculator of
GeoGebra GmbH [2024]
to search for the optimal value.
We plotted the value functions for finding the optimal agent and nature policies separately.
In both cases, we look for the policy values that optimize the worst-case scenario from the player’s perspective.
Once we found the value that both players can achieve regardless of the other player’s policy, we found the Nash equilibrium value and policies.
The models used for finding the optimal values and policies can be found at
https://github.com/LAVA-LAB/RPOMDP_game_semantics_value_functions
.

The computed optimal values show that the optimal values differ between the RPOMDPs in the tuples.
These tuples of RPOMDPs therefore prove Theorem
1
.

After the optimal value computation, we discuss the structural differences of the equivalent POSGs.
Although the structural differences between two POSGs do not ensure that they have a different optimal value, the differences do provide an intuition in the cases where we know that the optimal values differ.

D.1
Stickiness Matters

We first revisit the RPOMDP in
Figure

2
and show how we computed the optimal values to show that stickiness matters in RPOMDPs.

Figure 7
:
Representation of the split used in the construction of value function of the RPOMDP in
Figure

.

We show that we can reason with deterministic nature policies by showing that the value functions are linear in the deterministic nature policies.
Combining this with the convexity of the uncertainty sets, we show that any finite probability distribution over the deterministic nature policies,
i.e.
, any mixed nature policy, can be rewritten as another deterministic nature policy that is contained in the policy set.
We can, therefore, limit ourselves to searching for the optimal policy in the deterministic nature policy set.
We first prove the following lemma:

Lemma 1
.

Given the full stickiness and zero stickiness RPOMDPs
M_{1}
and
M_{2}
of
Figure

:

\forall\theta^{mix}\in\Theta^{mix},\exists\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{det},\forall\pi\in\Pi.\;V_{\text{fh}}^{M_{1}}(\pi,\theta^{mix})=V_{\text{fh}}^{M_{1}}(\pi,\theta^{det}),

\forall\theta^{mix}\in\Theta^{mix},\exists\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{det},\forall\pi\in\Pi.\;V_{\text{fh}}^{M_{2}}(\pi,\theta^{mix})=V_{\text{fh}}^{M_{2}}(\pi,\theta^{det}).

Proof.

We focus on the full stickiness RPOMDP
M_{1}
.
The result for the zero stickiness RPOMDP
M_{2}
follows from the same steps.
Let
\theta^{mix}\in\Theta^{mix}
be an arbitrary mixed nature policy and
\pi\in\Pi
an arbitrary stochastic agent policy.

\displaystyle=V_{\text{fh}}^{M_{1}}(\pi,\theta^{mix}).

Now we have that:

\forall\pi\in\Pi.\;V_{\text{fh}}^{M_{1}}(\pi,\theta^{mix})=V_{\text{fh}}^{M_{1}}(\pi,\theta^{\prime{det}}),

So we can conclude that:

\forall\theta^{mix}\in\Theta^{mix},\exists\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{det},\forall\pi\in\Pi.\;V_{\text{fh}}^{M_{1}}(\pi,\theta^{mix})=V_{\text{fh}}^{M_{1}}(\pi,\theta^{det}).

∎

We can now prove the following theorem:

Proposition 3
.

Given the full stickiness and zero stickiness RPOMDPs
M_{1}
and
M_{2}
of
Figure

:

\sup_{\pi\in\Pi}\inf_{\theta^{mix}\in\Theta^{mix}}V_{\text{fh}}^{M_{1}}(\pi,\theta^{mix})=\sup_{\pi\in\Pi}\inf_{\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{det}}V_{\text{fh}}^{M_{1}}(\pi,\theta^{det}),

\sup_{\pi\in\Pi}\inf_{\theta^{mix}\in\Theta^{mix}}V_{\text{fh}}^{M_{2}}(\pi,\theta^{mix})=\sup_{\pi\in\Pi}\inf_{\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{det}}V_{\text{fh}}^{M_{2}}(\pi,\theta^{det}).

Proof.

For both
M_{1}
and
M_{2}
, the
\leq
direction directly follows from
Lemma

1
and the
\geq
direction from
\Theta^{det}\subseteq\Theta^{mix}
.
∎

Proposition

3

D.1.1
Underlying POSGs

Figure

(restated below) depicts the first couple of states of the full and zero stickiness POSGs of the RPOMDP in
Figure

.
We briefly discuss the structural differences.
In the zero stickiness case, we have an infinite action choice for nature at every nature state, but every choice will reach the same unrestricted agent states, as variable assignments never stick in the zero stickiness case.
Due to this, the state space of the zero stickiness POSG is finite, consisting of
S+S\times A
states, where
S
is the set of states and
A
is the set of actions of the original RPOMDP.
This can be seen in
Figure

at nature state
\langle s_{1},\{\},\bot\rangle
, where each choice reaches the same agent states
\langle s_{2},\{\}\rangle
and
\langle s_{3},\{\}\rangle
.
At this point, the choice does not influence the transition probability, so all choices go to the agent states with exactly the same probability and essentially have no influence.
This is no longer the case at nature states
\langle s_{4},\{\},\bot\rangle
and
\langle s_{5},\{\},\bot\rangle
, where the values chosen for
p
and
q
directly influence the probability of reaching agent state
\langle s_{6},\{\}\rangle,\langle s_{7},\{\}\rangle,\langle s_{8},\{\}\rangle
, and
\langle s_{9},\{\}\rangle
.

In the full stickiness case, on the other hand, each of the infinite action choices at the first nature state
\langle s_{1},\{\},\bot\rangle
leads to a
unique
continuation of the POSG, as each game continues to agent states with different restrictions on nature’s choice.
The full stickiness case, hence, has an infinite state space but only one infinite action choice, namely the first.

D.2.1
Underlying POSGs

The POSG of the full stickiness interpretation of the RPOMDP in
Figure

8
displays the same structural difference with the observation-based stickiness and zero stickiness interpretations as in
Figure

.
The variable assignment chosen at the first nature state
\langle s_{1},\{\},\bot\rangle
sticks in the full stickiness RPOMDP but not in the observation-based one zero stickiness ones.

The difference between the observation-based stickiness and zero stickiness POSGs occurs at a later stage, namely at nature states
\langle s4,\{\},\bot\rangle
and
\langle s5,\{\},\bot\rangle
.
After one of these states, the observation-based stickiness model follows the same structure as the full stickiness model, leading to infinitely many agent states with different variable restrictions.
The POSG of the zero stickiness interpretation continues with infinitely many transitions going to the same agent states
\langle s_{6},\{\}\rangle,\langle s_{7},\{\}\rangle,\langle s_{8},\{\}\rangle
, and
\langle s_{9},\{\}\rangle
with the totally undefined variable restriction.

D.3.1
Underlying POSGs

Figure

(restated below) depicts the agent first and nature first POSGs of the RPOMDP in
Figure

.
We briefly discuss the structural differences.
As the agent has a finite choice of actions, this will always lead to a finite split in the POSG.
Nature’s number of choices depends on the variable restrictions in the nature state.
In this simple model, we only have unrestricted, and hence infinite, nature choices.
The structural difference between the two POSGs is caused entirely by the order of play.

When the agent chooses first, the POSG has a finite number of states.
The infinite choice in the nature states
\langle s_{1},\{\},a\rangle
and
\langle s_{1},\{\},b\rangle
all lead to the same reward states, just with different probabilities determined by the chosen variable assignment.

When nature chooses first, we get an infinite number of agent states after nature’s infinite choice in nature state
\langle s_{1},\{\}\rangle
, as the chosen variable assignment needs to be recorded for the transition after the agent’s choice.
The number of states in the nature first model is hence infinite.
Each resulting agent state only has a finite choice leading to the same reward states.

Appendix E
Nature First Semantics

Throughout the main paper and the appendix, the definitions and proofs are all written with the agent first order of play.
This appendix discusses the changes required to achieve the same results with the nature first semantics.

Policies in the RPOMDP.

When nature moves first, nature receives the agent’s action after choosing its own action.
Therefore, nature policies in nature first RPOMDPs are of the following types:

\begin{aligned} \text{Stochastic:}\\
\text{Deterministic:}\\
\text{Mixed:}\end{aligned}\qquad\begin{aligned} \theta\colon&H^{{\mathfrak{n}},M}\to\Delta(\bm{U}),\\
\theta^{det}\colon&H^{{\mathfrak{n}},M}\to\bm{U},\\
\theta^{mix}\in&\;\Delta(H^{{\mathfrak{n}},M}\to\bm{U}).\end{aligned}

The agent policies do not change, as we assume the agent still cannot observe the variable assignments nature chooses.

Nature first POSG.

Given a nature first RPOMDP, we define its POSG as follows.

Definition 18

(Equivalent nature first POSG)
.

Given a robust POMDP
\langle S,A,\bm{T},R,Z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}},Z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},Z_{\circ},O^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},O^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},O_{\circ}\rangle
, we define the POSG where nature chooses first as a tuple
\langle\mathcal{S^{\mathfrak{a}},S^{\mathfrak{n}},A^{\mathfrak{a}},A^{\mathfrak{n}},T,R,Z^{\mathfrak{a}},Z^{\mathfrak{n}},O^{\mathfrak{a}},O^{\mathfrak{n}}}\rangle
, where

\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{n}},\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{a}},\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{n}},\mathcal{Z}^{\mathfrak{a}}
, and
\mathcal{Z}^{\mathfrak{n}}
remain the same as in
Definition

5
.
The agent’s state-space is given by
\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{a}}=S\times\bm{U}^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}\times\bm{U}
, and the transition, reward, and observation functions are defined as follows:

•

\mathcal{T}^{\mathfrak{a}}\colon\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{a}}\times\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{a}}\to\Delta(\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{n}})
, by
\mathcal{T^{\mathfrak{a}}}(\langle s,u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}},u\rangle,a,\langle s^{\prime},\mathsf{upd}(u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}},u,O^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet}(s),O_{\circ}(s),a),a\rangle)=\bm{T}(u)(s,a,s^{\prime})
.

•

\mathcal{T}^{\mathfrak{n}}\colon\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{n}}\times\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{n}}\to\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{a}}
, by
\mathcal{T^{\mathfrak{n}}}(\langle s,u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}},a\rangle,u,\langle s,u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}},u\rangle)=\begin{cases}1&\quad\text{if $u\in\bm{U}^{\mathcal{P}}(u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}})$,}\\
0&\quad\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

•

\mathcal{R\colon S^{\mathfrak{a}}\times A^{\mathfrak{a}}}\to\mathbb{R}
by
\mathcal{R}(\langle s,u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}},u\rangle,a)=R(s,a)
.

•

\mathcal{O}^{\mathfrak{a}}\colon(\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{a}}\cup\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{n}})\to\mathcal{Z}^{\mathfrak{a}}
by
\mathcal{O^{\mathfrak{a}}}(s)=\begin{cases}\langle O^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet}(s^{\prime}),O_{\circ}(s^{\prime})\rangle&\text{if $s=\langle s^{\prime},u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}},u\rangle\in\mathcal{S^{\mathfrak{a}}}$,}\\
\langle O^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet}(s^{\prime}),O_{\circ}(s^{\prime})\rangle&\text{if $s=\langle s^{\prime},u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}},a\rangle\in\mathcal{S^{\mathfrak{n}}}$.}\end{cases}

•

\mathcal{O}^{\mathfrak{n}}\colon(\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{a}}\cup\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{n}})\to\mathcal{Z}^{\mathfrak{n}}
by

\mathcal{O^{\mathfrak{n}}}(s)=\begin{cases}\langle O^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet}(s^{\prime}),O_{\circ}(s^{\prime}),\bot\rangle&\text{if $s=\langle s^{\prime},u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}},u\rangle\in\mathcal{S^{\mathfrak{a}}}$,}\\
\langle O^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet}(s^{\prime}),O_{\circ}(s^{\prime}),a\rangle&\text{if $s=\langle s^{\prime},u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}},a\rangle\in\mathcal{S^{\mathfrak{n}}}$.}\end{cases}

The
a
observed in a
\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{n}}
state corresponds to the previously chosen
a
.
So, the action that nature observes in a nature state
\langle s^{\prime},u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}},a\rangle\in\mathcal{S^{\mathfrak{n}}}
is the action
a\in A
that was taken to reach the current state
s^{\prime}\in S
of the RPOMDP, not the action the agent will take from the current state.
This game starts in a
\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{n}}
state consisting of the initial state
s_{I}\in S
in the RPOMDP, the totally undefined variable assignment
u^{\bot}\in\bm{U}^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}
, and a placeholder for the action
\bot
.

Paths and histories.

When reasoning with the nature first semantics, the order of the paths in the POSG changes:

\text{Paths}^{G}:(\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{a}}\times\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{a}}\times\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{n}}\times\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{n}})^{*}\times\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{a}}\Longrightarrow(\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{n}}\times\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{n}}\times\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{a}}\times\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{a}})^{*}\times\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{n}}.

As a result, the histories similarly change:

H^{G}:(\mathcal{Z}^{\mathfrak{a}}\times\mathcal{Z}^{\mathfrak{n}}\times\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{a}}\times\mathcal{Z}^{\mathfrak{a}}\times\mathcal{Z}^{\mathfrak{n}}\times\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{n}})^{*}\times\mathcal{Z}^{\mathfrak{a}}\times\mathcal{Z}^{\mathfrak{n}}\Longrightarrow(\mathcal{Z}^{\mathfrak{n}}\times\mathcal{Z}^{\mathfrak{a}}\times\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{n}}\times\mathcal{Z}^{\mathfrak{n}}\times\mathcal{Z}^{\mathfrak{a}}\times\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{a}})^{*}\times\mathcal{Z}^{\mathfrak{n}}\times\mathcal{Z}^{\mathfrak{a}}.

H^{{\mathfrak{a}},G}:(\mathcal{Z}^{\mathfrak{a}}\times\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{a}}\times\mathcal{Z}^{\mathfrak{a}})^{*}\times\mathcal{Z}^{\mathfrak{a}}\Longrightarrow(\mathcal{Z}^{\mathfrak{a}}\times\mathcal{Z}^{\mathfrak{a}}\times\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{a}})^{*}\times\mathcal{Z}^{\mathfrak{a}}.

H^{{\mathfrak{n}},G}:(\mathcal{Z}^{\mathfrak{n}}\times\mathcal{Z}^{\mathfrak{n}}\times\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{n}})^{*}\times\mathcal{Z}^{\mathfrak{n}}\Longrightarrow(\mathcal{Z}^{\mathfrak{n}}\times\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{n}}\times\mathcal{Z}^{\mathfrak{n}})^{*}\times\mathcal{Z}^{\mathfrak{n}}.

Policies in the POSG

As the order of the paths and historis changed, the policy types also change.
The agent now observes an extra state, instead of nature.
Note that this extra observation contains no extra information for the agent, while it did for nature in the agent-first semantics.

\displaystyle\text{Stochastic:}

\displaystyle\pi\colon

\displaystyle H^{{\mathfrak{a}},G}\to\Delta(\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{a}})

\displaystyle\implies

\displaystyle\pi\colon

\displaystyle H^{{\mathfrak{a}},G}\times\mathcal{Z^{\mathfrak{a}}}\to\Delta(\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{a}}),

\displaystyle\text{Deterministic:}

\displaystyle\pi^{det}\colon

\displaystyle H^{{\mathfrak{a}},G}\to\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{a}}

\displaystyle\implies

\displaystyle\pi^{det}\colon

\displaystyle H^{{\mathfrak{a}},G}\times\mathcal{Z^{\mathfrak{a}}}\to\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{a}},

\displaystyle\text{Mixed:}

\displaystyle\pi^{mix}\in

\displaystyle\Delta(H^{{\mathfrak{a}},G}\to\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{a}})

\displaystyle\implies

\displaystyle\pi^{mix}\in

\displaystyle\Delta(H^{{\mathfrak{a}},G}\times\mathcal{Z^{\mathfrak{a}}}\to\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{a}}),

\displaystyle\text{Stochastic:}

\displaystyle\theta\colon

\displaystyle H^{{\mathfrak{n}},G}\times\mathcal{Z^{\mathfrak{n}}}\to\Delta(\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{n}}),

\displaystyle\implies

\displaystyle\theta\colon

\displaystyle H^{{\mathfrak{n}},G}\to\Delta(\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{n}})

\displaystyle\text{Deterministic:}

\displaystyle\theta^{det}\colon

\displaystyle H^{{\mathfrak{n}},G}\times\mathcal{Z^{\mathfrak{n}}}\to\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{n}},

\displaystyle\implies

\displaystyle\theta^{det}\colon

\displaystyle H^{{\mathfrak{n}},G}\to\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{n}}

\displaystyle\text{Mixed:}

\displaystyle\theta^{mix}\in

\displaystyle\Delta(H^{{\mathfrak{n}},G}\times\mathcal{Z^{\mathfrak{n}}}\to\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{n}})

\displaystyle\implies

\displaystyle\theta^{mix}\in

\displaystyle\Delta(H^{{\mathfrak{n}},G}\to\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{n}}).

Additional adaptations.

At the end of
Appendices

A
,
F
and
G
, the adjustments required for the definitions or proofs to work with the nature first semantics are briefly discussed.

Appendix F
Equivalent Values

Given the stickiness and order of play, we show that the value of an RPOMDP and its POSG are equivalent (
Theorem

2
).
To do so, we construct a bijection between the sets of paths of the two models.
We use this bijection to subsequently construct new bijections between the sets of histories and policies and finally conclude that the values are equivalent.
For convenience, we repeat the proposition from the main text and then split it into several lemmas.

Proposition 1
(Bijection between paths and histories)
.

Let
M
be an RPOMDP, and
G
the POSG of
M
.
There exists a bijection
f\colon\text{Paths}^{M}\to\text{Paths}^{G}
and bijections between individual players’ histories:

•

Let
H^{{\mathfrak{a}},M}
and
H^{{\mathfrak{a}},G}
be the set of all agent histories in
M
and
G
, respectively.
There exists a bijection
f^{{\mathfrak{a}},h}\colon H^{{\mathfrak{a}},M}\to H^{{\mathfrak{a}},G}
.

•

Let
H^{{\mathfrak{n}},M}
and
H^{{\mathfrak{n}},G}
be the set of all nature histories in
M
and
G
, respectively.
There exists a bijection
f^{{\mathfrak{n}},h}\colon H^{{\mathfrak{n}},M}\to H^{{\mathfrak{n}},G}
.

Lemma 2

(Bijection between paths)
.

Let
M
be an RPOMDP, and
G
the POSG of
M
.
There exists a bijection
f\colon\text{Paths}^{M}\to\text{Paths}^{G}
.

Proof.

Let
\text{Paths}^{M,\ltimes}\subseteq(S\times A\times\bm{U})^{*}\times S^{?}
with
?\in\{0,1\}
be the set of all path segments in the RPOMDP, and let
\text{Paths}^{G,\ltimes}\subseteq(\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{a}}\times\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{a}}\times\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{n}}\times\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{n}})^{*}\times(\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{a}})^{?}
with
?\in\{0,1\}
be the set of all path segments in the POSG.
With path segment we mean that the path can starts at any time steps
t\in\mathbb{N}
and can end at any time step
t^{\prime}\in\mathbb{N},t<=t^{\prime}
.
The optional last state is only used for path segments until the horizon.
Note that
\text{Paths}^{M}\subseteq\text{Paths}^{M,\ltimes}
and
\text{Paths}^{G}\subseteq\text{Paths}^{G,\ltimes}
.
Let
\tau^{M}=\langle s_{0},a_{0},u_{0},s_{1},\dots,s_{n}\rangle\in\text{Paths}^{M}
and
t\leq n
, then
\tau^{M}(t)
indicates the
t
-th segment
\langle s_{t},a_{t},u_{t}\rangle
of
\tau^{M}
.
Note that if
t=n
, the segment will only consist of the final state
\langle s_{n}\rangle
.
Similarly, let
\tau^{G}=\langle s^{\mathfrak{a}}_{0},a^{\mathfrak{a}}_{0},s^{\mathfrak{n}}_{0},a^{\mathfrak{n}}_{0},s^{\mathfrak{a}}_{1},\dots,s^{\mathfrak{a}}_{n}\rangle=\langle\langle s_{0},u^{\bot}\rangle,a_{0},\langle s_{0},u^{\bot},a_{0}\rangle,u_{0},\langle s_{1},u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{1}\rangle,\dots,\langle s_{n},u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{n}\rangle\rangle\in\text{Paths}^{G}
and
t\leq n
, then
\tau^{G}(t)
indicates the
t
-th segment
\langle s^{\mathfrak{a}}_{t},a^{\mathfrak{a}}_{t},s^{\mathfrak{n}}_{t},a^{\mathfrak{n}}_{t}\rangle=\langle\langle s_{t},u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{t}\rangle,a_{t},\langle s_{t},u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{t},a_{t}\rangle,u_{t}\rangle
of
\tau^{G}
.
Note that if
t=n
, the segment will only consist of the final agent state
\langle s^{\mathfrak{a}}_{n}\rangle=\langle\langle s_{n},u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{n}\rangle\rangle
.

Let
g\colon\text{Paths}^{M,\ltimes}\times\bm{U}^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}\hookrightarrow\text{Paths}^{G,\ltimes}
defined by:

\displaystyle g(\langle s\rangle,u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}})

\displaystyle=\langle\langle s,u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}\rangle\rangle.

\displaystyle g(\langle s,a,u\rangle,u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\langle\langle s,u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}\rangle,a,\langle s,u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}},a\rangle,u\rangle&\text{ if }u\in\bm{U}^{\mathcal{P}}(u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}),\\
\bot&\text{ otherwise.}\end{cases}

\displaystyle g(\langle s,a,u\rangle\oplus{\tau^{M}}^{\prime},u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}g(\langle s,a,u\rangle,u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}})\oplus g({\tau^{M}}^{\prime},\mathsf{upd}(u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}},u,O^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet}(s),O_{\circ}(s),a))&\text{ if }u\in\bm{U}^{\mathcal{P}}(u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}),\\
\bot&\text{ otherwise.}\end{cases}

Let
f\colon\text{Paths}^{M}\to\text{Paths}^{G}
defined by:

\displaystyle f(\langle s\rangle)

\displaystyle=\langle\langle s,u^{\bot}\rangle\rangle.

\displaystyle f(\langle s,a,u\rangle)

\displaystyle=\langle\langle s,u^{\bot}\rangle,a,\langle s,u^{\bot},a\rangle,u\rangle.

\displaystyle f(\langle s,a,u\rangle\oplus{\tau^{M}}^{\prime})

\displaystyle=f(\langle s,a,u\rangle)\oplus g({\tau^{M}}^{\prime},\mathsf{upd}(u^{\bot},u,O^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet}(s),O_{\circ}(s),a)).

Where
u^{\bot}\in\bm{U}^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}
is the totally undefined function.
Note that the results of
f
and
g
are in
\text{Paths}^{G}
and
\text{Paths}^{G,\ltimes}
by construction.
Also, note that any call to
g
that originated from a call in
f
will have a result by construction.

We show that
f
is a bijection, meaning
f
is injective and surjective.
We first show
f
is injective, so we show that:

\forall\tau^{1,M},\tau^{2,M}\in\text{Paths}^{M}.\tau^{1,M}\neq\tau^{2,M}\implies f(\tau^{1,M})\neq f(\tau^{2,M}).

Given arbitrary
\tau^{1,M},\tau^{2,M}\in\text{Paths}^{M}
, we distinguish between the paths with superscripts
1
and
2
, respectively.
Assume
\tau^{1,M}\neq\tau^{2,M}
.
If
\tau^{1,M}
and
\tau^{2,M}
do not have the same horizon length, then neither do
f(\tau^{1,M})
and
f(\tau^{2,M})
.
Then trivially,
f(\tau^{1,M})\neq f(\tau^{2,M})
.

Assume
\tau^{1,M}
and
\tau^{2,M}
have the same horizon length
n
.
Then
\exists t\leq n
where
\tau^{1,M}
and
\tau^{2,M}
deviate, so
\tau^{1,M}(t)\neq\tau^{2,M}(t)
.
Let
q
be the smallest number where the paths deviate.
So
\forall t<q.\tau^{1,M}(t)=\tau^{2,M}(t)
and
\tau^{1,M}(q)\neq\tau^{2,M}(q)
.
Assume
q<n
.
Then we know
\langle s^{1}_{q},a^{1}_{q},u^{1}_{q}\rangle\neq\langle s^{2}_{q},a^{2}_{q},u^{2}_{q}\rangle
, which comes down to:
s^{1}_{q}\neq s^{2}_{q}\lor a^{1}_{q}\neq a^{2}_{q}\lor u^{1}_{q}\neq u^{2}_{q}
.

\displaystyle f(\tau^{1,M})

\displaystyle=f(\tau^{1,M}(1)\oplus{\tau^{1,M}}^{\prime})

\displaystyle=\tau^{1,G}(1)\oplus g({\tau^{1,M}}^{\prime},\mathsf{upd}(u^{\bot},u^{1}_{0},O^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet}(s^{1}_{0}),O_{\circ}(s^{1}_{0}),a^{1}_{0})).

Unfold
g
until
q
:

\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{t=0}^{q}(\tau^{1,G}(t))\oplus\langle\langle s^{1}_{q},\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{1,M}_{0:q})\rangle,a^{1}_{q},\langle s^{1}_{q},\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{1,M}_{0:q}),a^{1}_{q}\rangle,u^{1}_{q}\rangle\oplus g({\tau^{1,M}}^{\prime\prime},\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{1,M}_{0:q+1})).

Since
s^{1}_{q}\neq s^{2}_{q}\lor a^{1}_{q}\neq a^{2}_{q}\lor u^{1}_{q}\neq u^{2}_{q}
:

\displaystyle\neq\bigoplus_{t=0}^{q}(\tau^{1,G}(t))\oplus\langle\langle s^{2}_{q},\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{1,M}_{0:q})\rangle,a^{2}_{q},\langle s^{2}_{q},\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{1,M}_{0:q}),a^{2}_{q}\rangle,u^{2}_{q}\rangle\oplus g({\tau^{2,M}}^{\prime\prime},\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{1,M}_{0:q+1}))

\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{t=0}^{q}(\tau^{2,G}(t))\oplus\langle\langle s^{2}_{q},\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{2.M}_{0:q})\rangle,a^{2}_{q},\langle s^{2}_{q},\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{2,M}_{0:q}),a^{2}_{q}\rangle,u^{2}_{q}\rangle\oplus g({\tau^{2,M}}^{\prime\prime},\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{2,M}_{0:q+1})).

Fold
g
until
1
:

\displaystyle=\tau^{2,G}(1)\oplus g({\tau^{2,M}}^{\prime},\mathsf{upd}(u^{\bot},u^{2}_{0},O^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet}(s^{2}_{0}),O_{\circ}(s^{2}_{0}),a^{2}_{0}))

\displaystyle=f(\tau^{2,M}(1)\oplus{\tau^{2,M}}^{\prime})

\displaystyle=f(\tau^{2,M}).

If
q=n
, then the same result follows by removing everything after
\langle s^{1}_{q},\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{1,M}_{0:q})\rangle,\langle s^{2}_{q},\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{1,M}_{0:q})\rangle
, and
\langle s^{2}_{q},\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{2,M}_{0:q})\rangle
.
We thus have that
f(\tau^{1,M})\neq f(\tau^{2,M})
, so
f
is injective.

Next, we show that
f
is surjective, so we show that:

\forall\tau^{G}\in\text{Paths}^{G},\exists\tau^{M}\in\text{Paths}^{M}.f(\tau^{M})=\tau^{G}.

We show this holds by induction on the horizon length of the
\tau^{G}\in\text{Paths}^{G}
.
We write the length of
\tau^{G}
as
|\tau^{G}|
.

Assume
|\tau^{G}|=0
.
Then
\tau^{G}=\langle s_{I},u^{\bot}\rangle
.
We have that for
\langle s_{I}\rangle\in\text{Paths}^{M},f(\langle s_{I}\rangle)=\langle\langle s_{I},u^{\bot}\rangle\rangle=\tau^{G}
.
So for paths of horizon length
0
,
f
is surjective.

Now assume we know, given
q\in\mathbb{N},q\geq 1
, that:

\forall\tau^{G}\in\text{Paths}^{G}.|\tau^{G}|=q-1\implies\exists\tau^{M}\in\text{Paths}^{M}:f(\tau^{M})=\tau^{G}.

Take arbitrary
\tau^{G}\in\text{Paths}^{G}
with horizon length
|\tau^{G}|=q
.
Then we have
\tau^{G}=\tau^{G}_{0:q-1}\oplus\langle a_{q-1},\langle s_{q-1},u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{q-1},a_{q-1}\rangle,u_{q-1},\langle s_{q},u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{q}\rangle\rangle
.
Then
\tau^{G}_{0:q-1}\in\text{Paths}^{G}
and
|\tau^{G}_{0:q-1}|=q-1
.
By assumption, we get that:

\exists\tau^{M}_{0:q-1}\in\text{Paths}^{M},f(\tau^{M}_{0:q-1})=\tau^{G}_{0:q-1}.

Let
\tau^{M}_{0:q-1}\in\text{Paths}^{M}
such that
f(\tau^{M}_{0:q-1})=\tau^{G}_{0:q-1}
.
We then know that in
\tau^{G}
:

\forall t<q.u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{t}=\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{M}_{0:t}).

And, by
Definition

5
and the definition of
\text{Paths}^{G}
, that:

u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{q}=\mathsf{upd}(\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{M}_{0:q-1}),u_{q-1},O^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet}(s_{q-1}),O_{\circ}(s_{q-1}),a_{q-1}).

Let
\langle\langle s_{q-2},\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{M}_{0:q-2})\rangle,a_{q-2},\langle s_{q-2},\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{M}_{0:q-2}),a_{q-2}\rangle,u_{q-2},\langle s_{q-1},\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{M}_{0:q-1})\rangle\rangle
be the last two segments of
\tau^{G}_{0:q-1}
.
Then by definition and injectivity of
f
, we know that the last two segments of
\tau^{M}_{0:q-1}
are
\langle s_{q-2},a_{q-2},u_{q-2},s_{q-1}\rangle
.

Now, by definition
Definition

5
and the definition of
\text{Paths}^{G}
, we know that:

\tau^{G}=\tau^{G}_{0:q-1}\oplus\langle a_{q-1},\langle s_{q-1},u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{q-1},a_{q-1}\rangle,u_{q-1},\langle s_{q},u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{q}\rangle\rangle\in\text{Paths}^{G}

\Longleftrightarrow

\tau^{G}_{0:q-1}\in\text{Paths}^{G}\land\mathcal{T}^{\mathfrak{a}}(\langle s_{q-1},u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{q-1}\rangle,a_{q-1},\langle s_{q-1},u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{q-1},a_{q-1}\rangle)>0

\land\mathcal{T}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\langle s_{q-1},u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{q-1}),a_{q-1}\rangle,u_{q-1},\langle s_{q},u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{q}\rangle)>0

\Longleftrightarrow

\tau^{G}_{0:q-1}\in\text{Paths}^{G}\land u_{q-1}\in\bm{U}^{\mathcal{P}}(u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{q-1})\land\bm{T}(u_{q-1})(s_{q-1},a_{q-1},s_{q})>0

\Longleftrightarrow

\tau^{G}_{0:q-1}\in\text{Paths}^{G}\land u_{q-1}\in\bm{U}^{\mathcal{P}}(\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{M}_{0:q-1}))\land\bm{T}(u_{q-1})(s_{q-1},a_{q-1},s_{q})>0.

So, since
\tau^{G}\in\text{Paths}^{G}
, we know
u_{q-1}\in\bm{U}^{\mathcal{P}}(\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{M}_{0:q-1}))
and
\bm{T}(u_{q-1})(s_{q-1},a_{q-1},s_{q})>0
, which are the restrictions for
\tau^{M}=\tau^{M}_{0:q-1}\oplus\langle a_{q-1},u_{q-1},s_{q}\rangle\in\text{Paths}^{M}
to hold.

\displaystyle f(\tau^{M})

\displaystyle=f(\tau^{M}_{0:q-1}\oplus\langle a_{q-1},u_{q-1},s_{q}\rangle)

\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{t=0}^{q-2}\tau^{G}_{0:q-1}(t)\oplus g(\langle s_{q-1},a_{q-1},u_{q-1},s_{q}\rangle,\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{M}_{0:q-1}))

\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{t=0}^{q-2}\tau^{G}_{0:q-1}(t)\oplus g(\langle s_{q-1},a_{q-1},u_{q-1}\rangle,\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{M}_{0:q-1}))\oplus g(\langle s_{q}\rangle,\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{M}_{0:q}))

\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{t=0}^{q-2}\tau^{G}_{0:q-1}(t)\oplus g(\langle s_{q-1},a_{q-1},u_{q-1}\rangle,\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{M}_{0:q-1}))\oplus g(\langle s_{q}\rangle,\mathsf{upd}(\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{M}_{0:q-1}),u_{q-1},O^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet}(s_{q-1}),O_{\circ}(s_{q-1}),a_{q-1}))

\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{t=0}^{q-2}\tau^{G}_{0:q-1}(t)\oplus g(\langle s_{q-1},a_{q-1},u_{q-1}\rangle,\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{M}_{0:q-1}))\oplus g(\langle s_{q}\rangle,u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{q})

\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{t=0}^{q-2}\tau^{G}_{0:q-1}(t)\oplus\langle\langle s_{q-1},\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{M}_{0:q-1})\rangle,a_{q-1},\langle s_{q-1},\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{M}_{0:q-1}),a_{q-1}\rangle,u_{q-1}\rangle\oplus g(\langle s_{q}\rangle,u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{q})

\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{t=0}^{q-2}\tau^{G}_{0:q-1}(t)\oplus\langle\langle s_{q-1},u^{{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}}_{0:q-1}\rangle,a_{q-1},\langle s_{q-1},u^{{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}}_{q-1},a_{q-1}\rangle,u_{q-1}\rangle\oplus g(\langle s_{q}\rangle,u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{q})

\displaystyle=\tau^{G}_{0:q-1}\oplus\langle a_{q-1},\langle s_{q-1},u^{{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}}_{q-1},a_{q-1}\rangle,u_{q-1}\rangle\oplus g(\langle s_{q}\rangle,u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{q})

\displaystyle=\tau^{G}_{0:q-1}\oplus\langle a_{q-1},\langle s_{q-1},u^{{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}}_{q-1},a_{q-1}\rangle,u_{q-1},\langle s_{q},u^{{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}}_{q}\rangle\rangle

\displaystyle=\tau^{G}.

So if
f
is surjective for paths of arbitrary length
q-1\in\mathbb{N}
,
f
is surjective for paths of length
q
.
Hence, by induction,
f
is surjective.

f
is injective and surjective, hence
f
is a bijection.
∎

We write
\simeq
to indicate equivalence between objects in the RPOMDP and the POSG.

Corollary 1

(Corresponding paths)
.

f
is a bijection between
\text{Paths}^{M}
and
\text{Paths}^{G}
, so the set of paths in the RPOMDP is equivalent to the set of paths in the POSG:

\text{Paths}^{M}\simeq\text{Paths}^{G},\vskip-2.84526pt

where
\forall\tau^{M}\in\text{Paths}^{M},\forall\tau^{G}\in\text{Paths}^{G}.

\tau^{M}\simeq\tau^{G}\Longleftrightarrow f(\tau^{M})=\tau^{G}.

We show and prove a bijection between joint histories, as introduced in
Section

A.2
.
The individual agent and nature histories’ bijection proofs follow the same line of reasoning, omitting elements private to the other player.

Proposition 4

(Bijection between joint histories)
.

Let
M
be an RPOMDP, and
G
the POSG of
M
.
There exists a bijection
f^{h}\colon H^{M}\to H^{G}
.

Proof.

Let
H^{M,\ltimes}
be the joint histories segments for the RPOMDP and let
H^{G,\ltimes}
be the joint histories segments for the parameterized POSG.
Again, we have that
H^{M}\subseteq H^{M,\ltimes}
and
H^{G}\subseteq H^{G,\ltimes}
.
Let
h^{M}=\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet,0},z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet,0},z_{\circ,0},a_{0},u_{0},z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet,1},z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet,1},z_{\circ,1},\dots,z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet,n},z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet,n},z_{\circ,n}\rangle\in H^{M}
and
t\leq n
, then
h^{M}(t)
indicates the
t
-th segment
\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet,t},z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet,t},z_{\circ,t},a_{t},u_{t}\rangle
of
h^{M}
.
Note that if
t=n
, the segment will only consist of the final observations
\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet,n},z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet,n},z_{\circ,n}\rangle
.
Similarly, let
h^{G}=\langle\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet,0},z_{\circ,0}\rangle,\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet,0},z_{\circ,0},\bot\rangle,a_{0},\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet,0},z_{\circ,0}\rangle,\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet,0},z_{\circ,0},a_{0}\rangle,u_{0},\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet,1},z_{\circ,1}\rangle,\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet,1},z_{\circ,1},\bot\rangle,\dots,\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet,n},z_{\circ,n}\rangle,\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet,n},z_{\circ,n},\bot\rangle\rangle\in H^{G}
and
t\leq n
, then
h^{G}(t)
indicates the
t
-th segment
\langle\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet,t},z_{\circ,t}\rangle,\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet,t},z_{\circ,t},\bot\rangle,a_{t},\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet,t},z_{\circ,t}\rangle,\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet,t},z_{\circ,t},a_{t}\rangle,u_{t}\rangle
of
h^{G}
.
Note that if
t=n
, the segment will only consist of the final observations
\langle\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet,n},z_{\circ,n}\rangle,\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet,n},z_{\circ,n},\bot\rangle\rangle
.

Let
g^{h}\colon H^{M,\ltimes}\to H^{G,\ltimes}
defined by:

\displaystyle g^{h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle)

\displaystyle=\langle\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle,\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},\bot\rangle\rangle.

\displaystyle g^{h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a,u\rangle)

\displaystyle=\langle\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle,\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},\bot\rangle,a,\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle,\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a\rangle,u\rangle.

\displaystyle g^{h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a,u\rangle\oplus h^{\prime})

\displaystyle=g^{h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a,u\rangle)\oplus g^{h}(h^{\prime}).

Let
f^{h}\colon H^{M}\to H^{G}
defined by:

\displaystyle f^{h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle)

\displaystyle=\langle\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle,\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},\bot\rangle\rangle.

\displaystyle f^{h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a,u\rangle)

\displaystyle=\langle\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle,\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},\bot\rangle,a,\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle,\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a\rangle,u\rangle.

\displaystyle f^{h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a,u\rangle\oplus h^{\prime})

\displaystyle=f^{h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a,u\rangle)\oplus g^{h}(h^{\prime}).

Note that the results of
f^{h}
and
g^{h}
are in
H^{G}
and
H^{G,\ltimes}
by construction. Also, note that these function definitions are similar to those for paths.

We show that
f^{h}
is a bijection.
We first show
f^{h}
is injective, so we show that:

\forall h^{1,M},h^{2,M}\in H^{M}.h^{1,M}\neq h^{2,M}\implies f^{h}(h^{1,M})\neq f^{h}(h^{2,M}).

Given arbitrary
h^{1,M},h^{2,M}\in H^{M}
, we distinguish between the histories with a superscript
1,2
respectively.
Assume
h^{1,M}\neq h^{2,M}
.
If
h^{1,M}
and
h^{2,M}
do not have the same horizon length, then neither do
f^{h}(h^{1,M})
and
f^{h}(h^{2,M})
.
Then trivially,
f^{h}(h^{1,M})\neq f^{h}(h^{2,M})
.

Assume
f^{h}(h^{1,M})
and
f^{h}(h^{2,M})
have the same horizon length
n
.
Then
\exists t\leq n
where
f^{h}(h^{1,M})
and
f^{h}(h^{2,M})
deviate, so
h^{1,M}(t)\neq h^{2,M}(t)
.
Let
q
be the smallest number where the histories deviate.
So
\forall t<q.h^{1,M}(t)=h^{2,M}(t)
and
h^{1,M}(q)\neq h^{2,M}(q)
.
Assume
q<n
.
Then we know
\langle z^{{\mathfrak{a}},1}_{\bullet,q},z^{{\mathfrak{n}},1}_{\bullet,q},z^{1}_{\circ,q},a^{1}_{q},u^{1}_{q}\rangle\neq\langle z^{{\mathfrak{a}},2}_{\bullet,q},z^{{\mathfrak{n}},2}_{\bullet,q},z^{2}_{\circ,q},a^{2}_{q},u^{2}_{q}\rangle
, which comes down to:
z^{{\mathfrak{a}},1}_{\bullet,q}\neq z^{{\mathfrak{a}},2}_{\bullet,q}\lor z^{{\mathfrak{n}},1}_{\bullet,q}\neq z^{{\mathfrak{n}},2}_{\bullet,q}\lor z^{1}_{\circ,q}\neq z^{2}_{\circ,q}\lor a^{1}_{q}\neq a^{2}_{q}\lor u^{1}_{q}\neq u^{2}_{q}
.

\displaystyle f^{h}(h^{1,M})

\displaystyle=f^{h}(h^{1,M}(1)\oplus{h_{1}^{M}}^{\prime})

\displaystyle=h_{1}^{G}(1)\oplus g^{h}({h^{1,M}}^{\prime}).

Unfold
g^{h}
until
q
:

\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{t=0}^{q-1}(h_{1}^{G}(t))\oplus\langle\langle z^{{\mathfrak{a}},1}_{\bullet,q},z^{1}_{\circ,q}\rangle,\langle z^{{\mathfrak{n}},1}_{\bullet,q},z^{1}_{\circ,q},\bot\rangle,a^{1}_{q},\langle z^{{\mathfrak{a}},1}_{\bullet,q},z^{1}_{\circ,q}\rangle,\langle z^{{\mathfrak{n}},1}_{\bullet,q},z_{\circ,q},a^{1}_{q}\rangle,u^{1}_{q}\rangle\oplus g^{h}({h^{1,M}}^{\prime\prime}).

Since
z^{{\mathfrak{a}},1}_{\bullet,q}\neq z^{{\mathfrak{a}},2}_{\bullet,q}\lor z^{{\mathfrak{n}},1}_{\bullet,q}\neq z^{{\mathfrak{n}},2}_{\bullet,q}\lor z^{1}_{\circ,q}\neq z^{2}_{\circ,q}\lor a^{1}_{q}\neq a^{2}_{q}\lor u^{1}_{q}\neq u^{2}_{q}
:

\displaystyle\neq\bigoplus_{t=0}^{q-1}(h_{1}^{G}(t))\oplus\langle\langle z^{{\mathfrak{a}},2}_{\bullet,q},z^{2}_{\circ,q}\rangle,\langle z^{{\mathfrak{n}},2}_{\bullet,q},z^{2}_{\circ,q},\bot\rangle,a^{2}_{q},\langle z^{{\mathfrak{a}},2}_{\bullet,q},z^{2}_{\circ,q}\rangle,\langle z^{{\mathfrak{n}},2}_{\bullet,q},z_{\circ,q},a^{2}_{q}\rangle,u^{2}_{q}\rangle\oplus g^{h}({h^{2,M}}^{\prime\prime})

\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{t=0}^{q-1}(h^{2,G}(t))\oplus\langle\langle z^{{\mathfrak{a}},2}_{\bullet,q},z^{2}_{\circ,q}\rangle,\langle z^{{\mathfrak{n}},2}_{\bullet,q},z^{2}_{\circ,q},\bot\rangle,a^{2}_{q},\langle z^{{\mathfrak{a}},2}_{\bullet,q},z^{2}_{\circ,q}\rangle,\langle z^{{\mathfrak{n}},2}_{\bullet,q},z_{\circ,q},a^{2}_{q}\rangle,u^{2}_{q}\rangle\oplus g^{h}({h^{2,M}}^{\prime\prime}).

Fold
g^{h}
until
1
:

\displaystyle=h^{2,G}(1)\oplus g^{h}({h^{2,M}}^{\prime})

\displaystyle=f^{h}(h^{2,M}(1)\oplus{h_{2}^{M}}^{\prime})

\displaystyle=f^{h}(h^{2,M}).

If
q=n
, then the same result follows by removing everything after
\langle z^{{\mathfrak{n}},1}_{\bullet,q},z^{1}_{\circ,q},\bot\rangle
, and
\langle z^{{\mathfrak{n}},2}_{\bullet,q},z^{2}_{\circ,q},\bot\rangle
.
We thus have that
f^{h}(h^{1,M})\neq f^{h}(h^{2,M})
, so
f^{h}
is injective.

Next, we show that
f^{h}
is surjective, so we show that:

\forall h^{G}\in H^{G},\exists h^{M}\in H^{M}.f^{h}(h^{M})=h^{G}.

Take arbitrary
h^{G}\in H^{G}
.
By construction of
H^{G}
,
O^{G}
(see
Section

A.2
) is surjective, so we know
\exists\tau^{G}\in\text{Paths}^{G},O^{G}(\tau^{G})=h^{G}
.
Take
\tau^{G}\in\text{Paths}^{G}
such that
O^{G}(\tau^{G})=h^{G}
.
Let
\tau^{M}\in\text{Paths}^{M}
be the corresponding path in the RPOMDP.
So
f(\tau^{M})=\tau^{G}
.
Then
h^{M}=O^{M}(\tau^{M})\in H^{M}
.

We proof
f^{h}(h^{M})=h^{G}
by contradiction.
Assume
f^{h}(h^{M})=h_{2}^{G}\neq h^{G}
.
By construction of
f
, we know
|\tau^{M}|=|\tau^{G}|
.
Then, by construction of
O^{M}
,
O^{G}
, and
f^{h}
, which each map a segment to a segment, we know
|h_{2}^{G}|=|h^{G}|
.

Let
n
be the horizon length of
h_{2}^{G}
and
h^{G}
.
Then
\exists t\in\mathbb{N}
where
h_{2}^{G}
and
h^{G}
deviate, so
h^{G}(t)\neq h_{2}^{G}(t)
.
Let
q
be such a number where the horizons deviate.
So
h^{G}(q)\neq h_{2}^{G}(q)
.
Note that
q\geq 1
, since there is only one initial state, therefore
h^{G}(0)=h_{2}^{G}(0)
.
Assume
q<n
and let
\tau^{G}(q)=\langle\langle s_{q},u^{{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}}_{q}\rangle,a_{q},\langle s_{q},u^{{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}}_{q},a_{q}\rangle,u_{q}\rangle
.
Then by the definition and bijectivity of
f
, we know
\tau^{M}(q)=\langle s_{q},a_{q},u_{q}\rangle
.
Furthermore, by construction, we know that
f^{h},g^{h},O^{G},O^{G,\ltimes},O^{M}
, and
O^{M,\ltimes}
all apply on the segments of the paths or histories separately.

\displaystyle h^{G}(q)

\displaystyle=O^{G}(\tau^{G}(q))

\displaystyle=O^{G}(\langle\langle s_{q},u^{{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}}_{q}\rangle,a_{q},\langle s_{q},u^{{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}}_{q},a_{q}\rangle,u_{q}\rangle)

\displaystyle=\langle\langle O^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet}(s_{q}),O_{\circ}(s_{q})\rangle,\langle O^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet}(s_{q}),O_{\circ}(s_{q}),\bot\rangle,a_{q},\langle O^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet}(s_{q}),O_{\circ}(s_{q})\rangle,\langle O^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet}(s_{q}),O_{\circ}(s_{q}),a_{q}\rangle,u_{q}\rangle.

\displaystyle h_{2}^{G}(q)

\displaystyle=f^{h}(O^{M}(\tau^{M}(q)))

\displaystyle=f^{h}(O^{M}(\langle s_{q},a_{q},u_{q}\rangle))

\displaystyle=f^{h}(\langle O^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet}(s_{q}),O^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet}(s_{q}),O_{\circ}(s_{q}),a_{q},u_{q}\rangle)

\displaystyle=\langle\langle O^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet}(s_{q}),O_{\circ}(s_{q})\rangle,\langle O^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet}(s_{q}),O_{\circ}(s_{q}),\bot\rangle,a_{q},\langle O^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet}(s_{q}),O_{\circ}(s_{q})\rangle,\langle O^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet}(s_{q}),O_{\circ}(s_{q}),a_{q}\rangle,u_{q}\rangle

\displaystyle=h^{G}(q).

Hence
\exists t\in\mathbb{N}:h^{G}(t)\neq h_{2}^{G}(t)
is false.
If
q=n
, the same result follows by removing everything from
a_{q}
.
We hence get that
f^{h}(h^{M})=h^{G}
, so
\exists h^{M}\in H^{M},f^{h}(h^{M})=h^{G}
, therefore
f^{h}
is surjective.

f^{h}
is injective and surjective, hence
f^{h}
is a bijection.
∎

Lemma 3

(Bijection between agent and nature histories)
.

Following
Proposition

4
, we get bijections for the agent and nature histories by omitting the private objects of the other player.
Let
g^{{\mathfrak{a}},h}\colon H^{{\mathfrak{a}},M,\ltimes}\to H^{{\mathfrak{a}},G,\ltimes}
defined by:

\displaystyle g^{{\mathfrak{a}},h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle)

\displaystyle=\langle\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle\rangle.

\displaystyle g^{{\mathfrak{a}},h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a\rangle)

\displaystyle=\langle\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle,a,\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle\rangle.

\displaystyle g^{{\mathfrak{a}},h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a,h^{\prime}\rangle)

\displaystyle=g^{{\mathfrak{a}},h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a\rangle)\oplus g^{{\mathfrak{a}},h}(h^{\prime}).

Let
f^{{\mathfrak{a}},h}\colon H^{{\mathfrak{a}},M}\to H^{{\mathfrak{a}},G}
defined by:

\displaystyle f^{{\mathfrak{a}},h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle)

\displaystyle=\langle\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle\rangle.

\displaystyle f^{{\mathfrak{a}},h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a\rangle)

\displaystyle=\langle\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle,a,\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle\rangle.

\displaystyle f^{{\mathfrak{a}},h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a,h^{\prime}\rangle)

\displaystyle=f^{{\mathfrak{a}},h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a\rangle)\oplus g^{{\mathfrak{a}},h}(h^{\prime}).

f^{{\mathfrak{a}},h}
is a bijection.

Let
g^{{\mathfrak{n}},h}\colon H^{{\mathfrak{n}},M,\ltimes}\to H^{{\mathfrak{n}},G,\ltimes}
defined by:

\displaystyle g^{{\mathfrak{n}},h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle)

\displaystyle=\langle\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},\bot\rangle\rangle.

\displaystyle g^{{\mathfrak{n}},h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a,u\rangle)

\displaystyle=\langle\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},\bot\rangle,\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a\rangle,u\rangle.

\displaystyle g^{{\mathfrak{n}},h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a,u,h^{\prime}\rangle)

\displaystyle=g^{{\mathfrak{n}},h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a,u\rangle)\oplus g^{{\mathfrak{n}},h}(h^{\prime}).

Let
f^{{\mathfrak{n}},h}\colon H^{{\mathfrak{n}},M}\to H^{{\mathfrak{n}},G}
defined by:

\displaystyle f^{{\mathfrak{n}},h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle)

\displaystyle=\langle\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},\bot\rangle\rangle.

\displaystyle f^{{\mathfrak{n}},h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a,u\rangle)

\displaystyle=\langle\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},\bot\rangle,\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a\rangle,u\rangle.

\displaystyle f^{{\mathfrak{n}},h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a,u,h^{\prime}\rangle)

\displaystyle=f^{{\mathfrak{n}},h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a,u\rangle)\oplus g^{{\mathfrak{n}},h}(h^{\prime}).

f^{{\mathfrak{n}},h}
is a bijection.

Corollary 2

(Corresponding histories)
.

f^{h}
is a bijection between
H^{M}
and
H^{G}
, so the set of histories in the RPOMDP is equivalent to the set of histories in the parameterized POSG:

H^{M}\simeq H^{G},

where
\forall h^{M}\in H^{M},\forall h^{G}\in H^{G}.

h^{M}\simeq h^{G}\Longleftrightarrow f^{h}(h^{M})=h^{G}.

Similarly:

H^{{\mathfrak{a}},M}\simeq H^{{\mathfrak{a}},G},

where
\forall h^{{\mathfrak{a}},M}\in H^{{\mathfrak{a}},M},\forall h^{{\mathfrak{a}},G}\in H^{{\mathfrak{a}},G}.

h^{{\mathfrak{a}},M}\simeq h^{{\mathfrak{a}},G}\Longleftrightarrow f^{{\mathfrak{a}},h}(h^{{\mathfrak{a}},M})=h^{{\mathfrak{a}},G}.

And:

H^{{\mathfrak{n}},M}\simeq H^{{\mathfrak{n}},G},

where
\forall h^{{\mathfrak{a}},M}\in H^{{\mathfrak{a}},M},\forall h^{{\mathfrak{a}},G}\in H^{{\mathfrak{a}},G}.

h^{{\mathfrak{a}},M}\simeq h^{{\mathfrak{a}},G}\Longleftrightarrow f^{{\mathfrak{a}},h}(h^{{\mathfrak{a}},M})=h^{{\mathfrak{a}},G}.

Proposition 2 from the main text is a direct corollary of the bijections between histories established above.
For completeness, we repeat the proposition here.

Proposition 2
(Bijection between policies)
.

Let
f^{\pi}\colon\Pi^{M}\to\Pi^{G}
defined by:

f^{\pi}(\pi^{M})(h^{{\mathfrak{a}},G})=\pi^{M}((f^{{\mathfrak{a}},h})^{-1}(h^{{\mathfrak{a}},G})),

then
f^{\pi}
is a bijection.

Let
f^{\theta}\colon\Theta^{M}\to\Theta^{G}
defined by:

f^{\theta}(\theta^{M})(h^{{\mathfrak{n}},G},\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a\rangle)=\theta^{M}((f^{{\mathfrak{n}},h})^{-1}(h^{{\mathfrak{n}},G}),a),

then
f^{\theta}
is a bijection.

Corollary 3

(Corresponding policies)
.

f^{\pi}
is a bijection between agent policies, so the set of agent policies in the RPOMDP is equivalent to the set of agent policies in the parameterized POSG:

\Pi^{M}\simeq\Pi^{G},

where
\forall\pi^{M}\in\Pi^{M},\forall\pi^{G}\in\Pi^{G}.

\pi^{M}\simeq\pi^{G}\Longleftrightarrow f^{\pi}(\pi^{M})=\pi^{G}.

Similarly:

\Theta^{M}\simeq\Theta^{G},

where
\forall\theta^{M}\in\Theta^{M},\forall\theta^{G}\in\Theta^{G}.

\theta^{M}\simeq\theta^{G}\Longleftrightarrow f^{\theta}(\theta^{M})=\theta^{G}.

See
2

Proof.

We prove
R(\tau^{M})=\mathcal{R}(\tau^{G})
for corresponding paths
\tau^{M},\tau^{G}
.
By definition of corresponding paths, we know that
\forall t\in\mathbb{N}.\tau^{G}(t)=g(\tau^{M}(t),u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{t-1})
.

\displaystyle R(\tau^{M})

\displaystyle=\sum_{t\in\mathbb{N}}R(\tau^{M}(t))

\displaystyle=\sum_{t\in\mathbb{N}}R(s_{t},a_{t},u_{t})

\displaystyle=\sum_{t\in\mathbb{N}}R(s_{t},a_{t})

\displaystyle=\sum_{t\in\mathbb{N}}\mathcal{R}(\langle s_{t},u^{{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}}_{t-1}\rangle,a_{t})

\displaystyle=\sum_{t\in\mathbb{N}}\mathcal{R}(\langle s_{t},u^{{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}}_{t-1}\rangle,a_{t},\langle s_{t},u^{{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}}_{t-1},a_{t}\rangle,u_{t})

\displaystyle=\sum_{t\in\mathbb{N}}\mathcal{R}(\tau^{G}(t))

\displaystyle=\mathcal{R}(\tau^{G}).

Now, since joint corresponding policies
\pi^{M},\theta^{M}
and
\pi^{G},\theta^{G}
lead to the same distribution over corresponding paths, we know that
V_{\phi}^{\pi^{M},\theta^{M}}=V_{\phi}^{\pi^{G},\theta^{G}}
.
∎

F.1
Mixed policies

Given the bijection between histories and stochastic policies, we can define a bijection between mixed policies similar to the one between stochastic policies.
Note that we apply the bijection between stochastic policies to deterministic policies.

Proposition 5

(Bijection between mixed policies)
.

Let
f^{\pi,{mix}}\colon\Pi^{M,{mix}}\to\Pi^{G,{mix}}
defined by:

f^{\pi,{mix}}(\pi^{M,{mix}})(\pi^{G,{det}})=\pi^{M,{mix}}((f^{\pi})^{-1}(\pi^{G,{det}})),

then
f^{\pi,{mix}}
is a bijection.

Let
f^{\theta,{mix}}\colon\Theta^{M,{mix}}\to\Theta^{G,{mix}}
defined by:

f^{\theta,{mix}}(\theta^{M,{mix}})(\theta^{G,{det}})=\theta^{M,{mix}}((f^{\theta})^{-1}(\theta^{G,{det}})),

then
f^{\theta,{mix}}
is a bijection.

Corollary 4

(Corresponding mixed policies)
.

f^{\pi,{mix}}
is a bijection between agent policies, so the set of mixed agent policies in the RPOMDP is equivalent to the set of mixed agent policies in the parameterized POSG:

\Pi^{M,{mix}}\simeq\Pi^{G,{mix}},

where
\forall\pi^{M,{mix}}\in\Pi^{M,{mix}},\forall\pi^{G,{mix}}\in\Pi^{G,{mix}}.

\pi^{M,{mix}}\simeq\pi^{G,{mix}}\Longleftrightarrow f^{\pi,{mix}}(\pi^{M,{mix}})=\pi^{G,{mix}}.

Similarly:

\Theta^{M,{mix}}\simeq\Theta^{G,{mix}},

where
\forall\theta^{M,{mix}}\in\Theta^{M,{mix}},\forall\theta^{G,{mix}}\in\Theta^{G,{mix}}.

\theta^{M,{mix}}\simeq\theta^{G,{mix}}\Longleftrightarrow f^{\theta,{mix}}(\theta^{M,{mix}})=\theta^{G,{mix}}.

Theorem 4

(Equivalent values mixed policies)
.

Let
M
be an RPOMDP, and
G
the POSG of
M
.
Let
\pi^{M,{mix}}\in\Pi^{M,{mix}},\pi^{G,{mix}}=f^{\pi,{mix}}(\pi^{M,{mix}})\in\Pi^{G,{mix}}
be corresponding agent policies, and
\theta^{M,{mix}}\in\Theta^{M,{mix}},\theta^{G,{mix}}=f^{\theta,{mix}}(\theta^{M,{mix}})\in\Theta^{G,{mix}}
be corresponding nature policies.
Then, their values for the RPOMDP and POSG coincide:

V_{\phi}^{\pi^{M,{mix}},\theta^{M,{mix}}}=V_{\phi}^{\pi^{G,{mix}},\theta^{G,{mix}}}.

The proof follows the same steps as for Theorem
2
for stochastic policies, where the distribution over corresponding paths now follows from the same distribution over corresponding deterministic policies, which in turn leads to the same distributions over corresponding paths.

F.2
Nature first

As explained in
Appendix

E
, when reasoning with nature first semantics, the paths of the POSGs change.
The bijections in this appendix start from the bijection between paths.
Below, we give the bijections for the nature first semantics that differ from the bijections for the agent first semantics.
The bijection proofs follow the same steps in the nature first case as in the agent first case.
We show the adjusted proof for the path bijection to illustrate how to deal with the delayed observation of the last agent action.

Lemma 4

(Nature first bijection between paths)
.

Let M be an RPOMDP, and G the POSG of M.
There exists a bijection
f\colon\text{Paths}^{M}\to\text{Paths}^{G}

Proof.

Let
\text{Paths}^{M,\ltimes}\subseteq(S\times A\times\bm{U})^{*}\times S^{?}
with
?\in\{0,1\}
be the set of all path segments in the RPOMDP, and let
\text{Paths}^{G,\ltimes}\subseteq\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{n}}\times\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{n}}\times\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{a}}\times\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{a}})^{*}\times(\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{n}})^{?}
with
?\in\{0,1\}
be the set of all path segments in the POSG.
With path segment we mean that the path can starts at any time steps
t\in\mathbb{N}
and can end at any time step
t^{\prime}\in\mathbb{N},t<=t^{\prime}
.
The optional last state is only used for path segments until the horizon.
Note that
\text{Paths}^{M}\subseteq\text{Paths}^{M,\ltimes}
and
\text{Paths}^{G}\subseteq\text{Paths}^{G,\ltimes}
.
Let
\tau^{M}=\langle s_{0},a_{0},u_{0},s_{1},\dots,s_{n}\rangle\in\text{Paths}^{M}
and
t\leq n
, then
\tau^{M}(t)
indicates the
t
-th segment
\langle s_{t},a_{t},u_{t}\rangle
of
\tau^{M}
.
Note that if
t=n
, the segment will only consist of the final state
\langle s_{n}\rangle
.
Similarly, let
\tau^{G}=\langle s^{\mathfrak{n}}_{0},a^{\mathfrak{n}}_{0},s^{\mathfrak{a}}_{0},a^{\mathfrak{a}}_{0},s^{\mathfrak{n}}_{1},\dots,s^{\mathfrak{n}}_{n}\rangle=\langle\langle s_{0},u^{\bot},\bot\rangle,u_{0},\langle s_{0},u^{\bot},u_{0}\rangle,a_{0},\langle s_{1},u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{1},a_{0}\rangle,\dots,\langle s_{n},u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{n},a_{n-1}\rangle\rangle\in\text{Paths}^{G}
and
t\leq n
, then
\tau^{G}(t)
indicates the
t
-th segment
\langle s^{\mathfrak{n}}_{t},a^{\mathfrak{n}}_{t},s^{\mathfrak{a}}_{t},a^{\mathfrak{a}}_{t}\rangle=\langle\langle s_{t},u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{t},a_{t-1}\rangle,u_{t},\langle s_{t},u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{t},u_{t}\rangle,a_{t}\rangle
of
\tau^{G}
.
Note that if
t=n
, the segment will only consist of the final nature state
\langle s^{\mathfrak{a}}_{n}\rangle=\langle\langle s_{n},u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{n},a_{n-1}\rangle\rangle
.

Let
g\colon\text{Paths}^{M,\ltimes}\times\bm{U}^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}\times A\hookrightarrow\text{Paths}^{G,\ltimes}
defined by:

\displaystyle g(\langle s\rangle,u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}},a)

\displaystyle=\langle\langle s,u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}},a^{\prime}\rangle\rangle.

\displaystyle g(\langle s,a,u\rangle,u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}},a^{\prime})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\langle\langle s,u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}},a^{\prime}\rangle,u,\langle s,u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}},u\rangle,a\rangle&\text{ if }u\in\bm{U}^{\mathcal{P}}(u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}),\\
\bot&\text{ otherwise.}\end{cases}

\displaystyle g(\langle s,a,u\rangle\oplus{\tau^{M}}^{\prime},u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}},a^{\prime})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}g(\langle s,a,u\rangle,u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}},a^{\prime})\oplus g({\tau^{M}}^{\prime},\mathsf{upd}(u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}},u,O^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet}(s),O_{\circ}(s),a),a)&\text{ if }u\in\bm{U}^{\mathcal{P}}(u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}),\\
\bot&\text{ otherwise.}\end{cases}

Let
f\colon\text{Paths}^{M}\to\text{Paths}^{G}
defined by:

\displaystyle f(\langle s\rangle)

\displaystyle=\langle\langle s,u^{\bot},\bot\rangle\rangle.

\displaystyle f(\langle s,a,u\rangle)

\displaystyle=\langle\langle s,u^{\bot},\bot\rangle,u,\langle s,u^{\bot},u\rangle,a\rangle.

\displaystyle f(\langle s,a,u\rangle\oplus{\tau^{M}}^{\prime})

\displaystyle=f(\langle s,a,u\rangle)\oplus g({\tau^{M}}^{\prime},\mathsf{upd}(u^{\bot},u,O^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet}(s),O_{\circ}(s),a),a).

Where
u^{\bot}\in\bm{U}^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}
is the totally undefined function.
Note that the results of
f
and
g
are in
\text{Paths}^{G}
and
\text{Paths}^{G,\ltimes}
by construction.
Also, note that any call to
g
that originated from a call in
f
will have a result by construction.

We show that
f
is a bijection, meaning
f
is injective and surjective.
We first show
f
is injective, so we show that:

\forall\tau^{1,M},\tau^{2,M}\in\text{Paths}^{M}.\tau^{1,M}\neq\tau^{2,M}\implies f(\tau^{1,M})\neq f(\tau^{2,M}).

Given arbitrary
\tau^{1,M},\tau^{2,M}\in\text{Paths}^{M}
, we distinguish between the paths with superscripts
1
and
2
, respectively.
Assume
\tau^{1,M}\neq\tau^{2,M}
.
If
\tau^{1,M}
and
\tau^{2,M}
do not have the same horizon length, then neither do
f(\tau^{1,M})
and
f(\tau^{2,M})
.
Then trivially,
f(\tau^{1,M})\neq f(\tau^{2,M})
.

Assume
\tau^{1,M}
and
\tau^{2,M}
have the same horizon length
n
.
Then
\exists t\leq n
where
\tau^{1,M}
and
\tau^{2,M}
deviate, so
\tau^{1,M}(t)\neq\tau^{2,M}(t)
.
Let
q
be the smallest number where the paths deviate.
So
\forall t<q.\tau^{1,M}(t)=\tau^{2,M}(t)
and
\tau^{1,M}(q)\neq\tau^{2,M}(q)
.
Assume
q<n
.
Then we know
\langle s^{1}_{q},a^{1}_{q},u^{1}_{q}\rangle\neq\langle s^{2}_{q},a^{2}_{q},u^{2}_{q}\rangle
, which comes down to:
s^{1}_{q}\neq s^{2}_{q}\lor a^{1}_{q}\neq a^{2}_{q}\lor u^{1}_{q}\neq u^{2}_{q}
.

\displaystyle f(\tau^{1,M})

\displaystyle=f(\tau^{1,M}(1)\oplus{\tau^{1,M}}^{\prime})

\displaystyle=\tau^{1,G}(1)\oplus g({\tau^{1,M}}^{\prime},\mathsf{upd}(u^{\bot},u^{1}_{0},O^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet}(s^{1}_{0}),O_{\circ}(s^{1}_{0}),a^{1}_{0}),a^{1}_{0}).

Unfold
g
until
q
:

\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{t=0}^{q}(\tau^{1,G}(t))\oplus\langle\langle s^{1}_{q},\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{1,M}_{0:q}),a^{1}_{q-1}\rangle,u^{1}_{q},\langle s^{1}_{q},\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{1,M}_{0:q}),u^{1}_{q}\rangle,a^{1}_{q}\rangle\oplus g({\tau^{1,M}}^{\prime\prime},\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{1,M}_{0:q+1}),a^{1}_{q})

Since
s^{1}_{q}\neq s^{2}_{q}\lor a^{1}_{q}\neq a^{2}_{q}\lor u^{1}_{q}\neq u^{2}_{q}
:

\displaystyle\neq\bigoplus_{t=0}^{q}(\tau^{1,G}(t))\oplus\langle\langle s^{2}_{q},\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{1,M}_{0:q}),a^{1}_{q-1}\rangle,u^{2}_{q},\langle s^{2}_{q},\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{1,M}_{0:q}),u^{2}_{q}\rangle,a^{2}_{q}\rangle\oplus g({\tau^{2,M}}^{\prime\prime},\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{1,M}_{0:q+1}),a^{2}_{q})

\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{t=0}^{q}(\tau^{2,G}(t))\oplus\langle\langle s^{2}_{q},\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{2.M}_{0:q}),a^{2}_{q-1}\rangle,u^{2}_{q},\langle s^{2}_{q},\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{2,M}_{0:q}),u^{2}_{q}\rangle,a^{2}_{q}\rangle\oplus g({\tau^{2,M}}^{\prime\prime},\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{2,M}_{0:q+1}),a^{2}_{q}).

Fold
g
until
1
:

\displaystyle=\tau^{2,G}(1)\oplus g({\tau^{2,M}}^{\prime},\mathsf{upd}(u^{\bot},u^{2}_{0},O^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet}(s^{2}_{0}),O_{\circ}(s^{2}_{0}),a^{2}_{0}),a^{2}_{0})

\displaystyle=f(\tau^{2,M}(1)\oplus{\tau^{2,M}}^{\prime})

\displaystyle=f(\tau^{2,M}).

If
q=n
, then the same result follows by removing everything after
\langle s^{1}_{q},\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{1,M}_{0:q}),a^{1}_{q-1}\rangle,\langle s^{2}_{q},\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{1,M}_{0:q}),a^{1}_{q-1}\rangle
, and
\langle s^{2}_{q},\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{2,M}_{0:q}),a^{2}_{q-1}\rangle
.
We thus have that
f(\tau^{1,M})\neq f(\tau^{2,M})
, so
f
is injective.

Next, we show that
f
is surjective, so we show that:

\forall\tau^{G}\in\text{Paths}^{G},\exists\tau^{M}\in\text{Paths}^{M}.f(\tau^{M})=\tau^{G}.

We show this holds by induction on the horizon length of the
\tau^{G}\in\text{Paths}^{G}
.
We write the length of
\tau^{G}
as
|\tau^{G}|
.

Assume
|\tau^{G}|=0
.
Then
\tau^{G}=\langle s_{I},u^{\bot}\rangle
.
We have that for
\langle s_{I}\rangle\in\text{Paths}^{M},f(\langle s_{I}\rangle)=\langle\langle s_{I},u^{\bot}\rangle\rangle=\tau^{G}
.
So for paths of horizon length
0
,
f
is surjective.

Now assume we know, given
q\in\mathbb{N},q\geq 1
, that:

\forall\tau^{G}\in\text{Paths}^{G}.|\tau^{G}|=q-1\implies\exists\tau^{M}\in\text{Paths}^{M}:f(\tau^{M})=\tau^{G}.

Take arbitrary
\tau^{G}\in\text{Paths}^{G}
with horizon length
|\tau^{G}|=q
.
Then we have
\tau^{G}=\tau^{G}_{0:q-1}\oplus\langle u_{q-1},\langle s_{q-1},u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{q-1},u_{q-1}\rangle,a_{q-1},\langle s_{q},u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{q},a_{q-1}\rangle\rangle
.
Then
\tau^{G}_{0:q-1}\in\text{Paths}^{G}
and
|\tau^{G}_{0:q-1}|=q-1
.
By assumption, we get that:

\exists\tau^{M}_{0:q-1}\in\text{Paths}^{M},f(\tau^{M}_{0:q-1})=\tau^{G}_{0:q-1}.

Let
\tau^{M}_{0:q-1}\in\text{Paths}^{M}
such that
f(\tau^{M}_{0:q-1})=\tau^{G}_{0:q-1}
.
We then know that in
\tau^{G}
:

\forall t<q.u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{t}=\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{M}_{0:t}).

And, by
Definition

18
and the definition of
\text{Paths}^{G}
, that:

u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{q}=\mathsf{upd}(\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{M}_{0:q-1}),u_{q-1},O^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet}(s_{q-1}),O_{\circ}(s_{q-1}),a_{q-1}).

Let
\langle\langle s_{q-2},\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{M}_{0:q-2}),a_{q-3}\rangle,u_{q-2},\langle s_{q-2},\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{M}_{0:q-2}),u_{q-2}\rangle,a_{q-2},\langle s_{q-1},\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{M}_{0:q-1}),a_{q-2}\rangle\rangle
be the last two segments of
\tau^{G}_{0:q-1}
.
Then by definition and injectivity of
f
, we know that the last two segments of
\tau^{M}_{0:q-1}
are
\langle s_{q-2},a_{q-2},u_{q-2},s_{q-1}\rangle
.

Now, by definition
Definition

18
and the definition of
\text{Paths}^{G}
, we know that:

\tau^{G}=\tau^{G}_{0:q-1}\oplus\langle u_{q-1},\langle s_{q-1},u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{q-1},u_{q-1}\rangle,a_{q-1},\langle s_{q},u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{q},a_{q-1}\rangle\rangle\in\text{Paths}^{G}

\Longleftrightarrow

\tau^{G}_{0:q-1}\in\text{Paths}^{G}\land\mathcal{T}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\langle s_{q-1},u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{q-1},a_{q-2}\rangle,u_{q-1},\langle s_{q-1},u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{q-1},u_{q-1}\rangle)>0

\land\mathcal{T}^{\mathfrak{a}}(\langle s_{q-1},u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{q-1}),u_{q-1}\rangle,a_{q-1},\langle s_{q},u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{q},a_{q-1}\rangle)>0

\Longleftrightarrow

\tau^{G}_{0:q-1}\in\text{Paths}^{G}\land u_{q-1}\in\bm{U}^{\mathcal{P}}(u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{q-1})\land\bm{T}(u_{q-1})(s_{q-1},a_{q-1},s_{q})>0

\Longleftrightarrow

\tau^{G}_{0:q-1}\in\text{Paths}^{G}\land u_{q-1}\in\bm{U}^{\mathcal{P}}(\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{M}_{0:q-1}))\land\bm{T}(u_{q-1})(s_{q-1},a_{q-1},s_{q})>0.

So, since
\tau^{G}\in\text{Paths}^{G}
, we know
u_{q-1}\in\bm{U}^{\mathcal{P}}(\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{M}_{0:q-1}))
and
\bm{T}(u_{q-1})(s_{q-1},a_{q-1},s_{q})>0
, which are the restrictions for
\tau^{M}=\tau^{M}_{0:q-1}\oplus\langle a_{q-1},u_{q-1},s_{q}\rangle\in\text{Paths}^{M}
to hold.

\displaystyle f(\tau^{M})

\displaystyle=f(\tau^{M}_{0:q-1}\oplus\langle a_{q-1},u_{q-1},s_{q}\rangle)

\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{t=0}^{q-2}\tau^{G}_{0:q-1}(t)\oplus g(\langle s_{q-1},a_{q-1},u_{q-1},s_{q}\rangle,\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{M}_{0:q-1}),a_{q-2})

\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{t=0}^{q-2}\tau^{G}_{0:q-1}(t)\oplus g(\langle s_{q-1},a_{q-1},u_{q-1}\rangle,\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{M}_{0:q-1}),a_{q-2})\oplus g(\langle s_{q}\rangle,\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{M}_{0:q}),a_{q-1})

\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{t=0}^{q-2}\tau^{G}_{0:q-1}(t)\oplus g(\langle s_{q-1},a_{q-1},u_{q-1}\rangle,\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{M}_{0:q-1}),a_{q-2})\oplus g(\langle s_{q}\rangle,\mathsf{upd}(\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{M}_{0:q-1}),u_{q-1},O^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet}(s_{q-1}),O_{\circ}(s_{q-1}),a_{q-1}),a_{q-1})

\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{t=0}^{q-2}\tau^{G}_{0:q-1}(t)\oplus g(\langle s_{q-1},a_{q-1},u_{q-1}\rangle,\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{M}_{0:q-1}),a_{q-2})\oplus g(\langle s_{q}\rangle,u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{q},a_{q-1})

\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{t=0}^{q-2}\tau^{G}_{0:q-1}(t)\oplus\langle\langle s_{q-1},\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{M}_{0:q-1}),a_{q-2}\rangle,u_{q-1},\langle s_{q-1},\mathsf{fix}(\tau^{M}_{0:q-1}),u_{q-1}\rangle,a_{q-1}\rangle\oplus g(\langle s_{q}\rangle,u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{q},a_{q-1})

\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{t=0}^{q-2}\tau^{G}_{0:q-1}(t)\oplus\langle\langle s_{q-1},u^{{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}}_{q-1},a_{q-2}\rangle,u_{q-1},\langle s_{q-1},u^{{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}}_{q-1},u_{q-1}\rangle,a_{q-1}\rangle\oplus g(\langle s_{q}\rangle,u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{q},a_{q-1})

\displaystyle=\tau^{G}_{0:q-1}\oplus\langle u_{q-1},\langle s_{q-1},u^{{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}}_{q-1},u_{q-1}\rangle,a_{q-1}\rangle\oplus g(\langle s_{q}\rangle,u^{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}_{q},a_{q-1})

\displaystyle=\tau^{G}_{0:q-1}\oplus\langle u_{q-1},\langle s_{q-1},u^{{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}}_{q-1},u_{q-1}\rangle,a_{q-1},\langle s_{q},u^{{\scalebox{0.5}[1]{$\hookrightarrow$}}}_{q},a_{q-1}\rangle\rangle

\displaystyle=\tau^{G}.

So if
f
is surjective for paths of arbitrary length
q-1\in\mathbb{N}
,
f
is surjective for paths of length
q
.
Hence, by induction,
f
is surjective.

f
is injective and surjective, hence
f
is a bijection.
∎

Corollary 5

(Nature first bijections between histories)
.

Let
g^{h}\colon H^{M,\ltimes}\times A\to H^{G,\ltimes}
defined by:

\displaystyle g^{h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle,a^{\prime})

\displaystyle=\langle\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a^{\prime}\rangle,\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle\rangle.

\displaystyle g^{h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a,u\rangle,a^{\prime})

\displaystyle=\langle\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a^{\prime}\rangle,\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle,u,\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},\bot\rangle,\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle,a\rangle.

\displaystyle g^{h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a,u\rangle\oplus h^{\prime},a^{\prime})

\displaystyle=g^{h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a,u\rangle,\bot)\oplus g^{h}(h^{\prime},a).

Let
f^{h}\colon H^{M}\to H^{G}
defined by:

\displaystyle f^{h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle)

\displaystyle=\langle\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},\bot\rangle,\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle\rangle.

\displaystyle f^{h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a,u\rangle)

\displaystyle=\langle\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},\bot\rangle,\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle,u,\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},\bot\rangle,\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle,a\rangle.

\displaystyle f^{h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a,u\rangle\oplus h^{\prime})

\displaystyle=f^{h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a,u\rangle)\oplus g^{h}(h^{\prime},a).

Let
g^{{\mathfrak{a}},h}\colon H^{{\mathfrak{a}},M,\ltimes}\to H^{{\mathfrak{a}},G,\ltimes}
defined by:

\displaystyle g^{{\mathfrak{a}},h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle)

\displaystyle=\langle\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle\rangle.

\displaystyle g^{{\mathfrak{a}},h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a\rangle)

\displaystyle=\langle\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle,\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle,a\rangle.

\displaystyle g^{{\mathfrak{a}},h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a,h^{\prime}\rangle)

\displaystyle=g^{{\mathfrak{a}},h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a\rangle)\oplus g^{{\mathfrak{a}},h}(h^{\prime}).

Let
f^{{\mathfrak{a}},h}\colon H^{{\mathfrak{a}},M}\to H^{{\mathfrak{a}},G}
defined by:

\displaystyle f^{{\mathfrak{a}},h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle)

\displaystyle=\langle\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle\rangle.

\displaystyle f^{{\mathfrak{a}},h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a\rangle)

\displaystyle=\langle\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle,\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle,a\rangle.

\displaystyle f^{{\mathfrak{a}},h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a,h^{\prime}\rangle)

\displaystyle=f^{{\mathfrak{a}},h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a\rangle)\oplus g^{{\mathfrak{a}},h}(h^{\prime}).

f^{{\mathfrak{a}},h}
is a bijection.

Let
g^{{\mathfrak{n}},h}\colon H^{{\mathfrak{n}},M,\ltimes}\times A\to H^{{\mathfrak{n}},G,\ltimes}
defined by:

\displaystyle g^{{\mathfrak{n}},h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle,a^{\prime})

\displaystyle=\langle\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a^{\prime}\rangle\rangle.

\displaystyle g^{{\mathfrak{n}},h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a,u\rangle,a^{\prime})

\displaystyle=\langle\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a^{\prime}\rangle,u,\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},\bot\rangle\rangle.

\displaystyle g^{{\mathfrak{n}},h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a,u,h^{\prime}\rangle,a^{\prime})

\displaystyle=g^{{\mathfrak{n}},h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a,u\rangle,a^{\prime})\oplus g^{{\mathfrak{n}},h}(h^{\prime},a).

Let
f^{{\mathfrak{n}},h}\colon H^{{\mathfrak{n}},M}\to H^{{\mathfrak{n}},G}
defined by:

\displaystyle f^{{\mathfrak{n}},h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle)

\displaystyle=\langle\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},\bot\rangle\rangle.

\displaystyle f^{{\mathfrak{n}},h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a,u\rangle)

\displaystyle=\langle\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},\bot\rangle,u,\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},\bot\rangle\rangle.

\displaystyle f^{{\mathfrak{n}},h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a,u,h^{\prime}\rangle)

\displaystyle=f^{{\mathfrak{n}},h}(\langle z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ},a,u\rangle)\oplus g^{{\mathfrak{n}},h}(h^{\prime},a).

f^{{\mathfrak{n}},h}
is a bijection.

The bijection between stochastic nature policies no longer involves an extra state observation, whereas the bijection between stochastic agent policy now does.
Note that the extra agent state observation for the inverse function for the agent policy bijection can be derived from the history input, as this observation is the same as the last nature state observation contained in that history.

Corollary 6

(Bijection between policies)
.

Let
f^{\pi}\colon\Pi^{M}\to\Pi^{G}
defined by:

f^{\pi}(\pi^{M})(h^{{\mathfrak{a}},G},\langle z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle)=\pi^{M}((f^{{\mathfrak{a}},h})^{-1}(h^{{\mathfrak{a}},G})),

then
f^{\pi}
is a bijection.

Let
f^{\theta}\colon\Theta^{M}\to\Theta^{G}
defined by:

f^{\theta}(\theta^{M})(h^{{\mathfrak{n}},G})=\theta^{M}((f^{{\mathfrak{n}},h})^{-1}(h^{{\mathfrak{n}},G})),

then
f^{\theta}
is a bijection.

Appendix G
Nash Equilibrium

This appendix contains all the proofs required to show the existence of a Nash equilibrium in our POSGs,
i.e.
,
Theorem

3
, restated below.
See
3

Throughout this appendix, we use the RPOMDP histories, paths, and policies, as these require simpler notation.
We refer to
Appendix

F
for the bijections between the RPOMDP and POSG paths, histories, and policies.

G.1
Sufficient Statistic

Where in POMDPs the history of the agent is enough to reason optimally, this is not the case for RPODMPs and their equivalent POSGs.
Apart from their own history, the players must also consider all possible histories of the other player.

We adjust the notion of occupancy state used in
Delage et al. [2023]
to work with the infinite nature action space of our RPOMDP and equivalent POSGs.
As mentioned in the introduction of this appendix, we use the RPOMDP notation.
Given
\pi_{0:t-1}\in\Pi_{0:t-1},\theta_{0:t-1}\in\Theta_{0:t-1}
,
Delage et al. [2023]
defines the occupancy state
\sigma_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t-1}}
as the probability distribution over all joint histories given agent and nature policies
\pi_{0:t-1}
and
\theta_{0:t-1}
.

\forall h_{t}\in H_{t}:\sigma_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t-1}}(h_{t})=\Pr(h_{t}\mid\pi_{0:t-1},\theta_{0:t-1}).

\sum_{h_{t}\in H_{t}}\sigma_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t-1}}(h_{t})=1.

In the original definition of the occupancy state, nature’s action space is finite.
This occupancy state is a sufficient statistic for computing the next occupancy state and the expected reward at time
t
given the next
\pi_{t}
and
\theta_{t}
in their POSG models.

However, as we deal with an infinite action space, we must make adjustments to ensure the subset of joint histories for each occupancy state is finite.
Therefore, we keep track of nature’s policy to be able to generate the finite subset of joint histories that the corresponding occupancy states have a distribution over.

Our version of the occupancy state extends the original occupancy state with the corresponding nature policy.
Given
\pi_{0:t-1}\in\Pi_{0:t-1},\theta_{0:t-1}\in\Theta_{0:t-1}
:

\text{OS}_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t-1}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\langle\sigma_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t-1}},\theta_{0:t-1}\rangle.

\forall h_{t}\in H_{t}:\sigma_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t-1}}{\theta_{0:t-1}}(h_{t})=\Pr(h_{t}\mid\pi_{0:t-1},\theta_{0:t-1}).

\sum_{h_{t}\in H_{t}}\sigma_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t-1}}(h_{t})=1.

We show that the occupancy state
\text{OS}_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t-1}}
together with agent and nature policies
\pi_{t},\theta_{t}
at time
t
, is a sufficient statistic for computing the next occupancy state
\text{OS}_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t}}
and the expected reward
\mathsf{R}(\text{OS}_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t-1}},\pi_{t},\theta_{t})=\mathbb{E}[r_{t}\mid\pi_{0:t-1},\pi_{t},\theta_{0:t-1},\theta_{t}]
.
Note that these proofs are based on the proofs in Appendix B of
Delage et al. [2023]
.

\displaystyle\text{OS}_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t}}(h_{t}\oplus\langle a_{t},u_{t},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},z_{\circ}\rangle)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\langle\sigma_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t}}(h_{t}\oplus\langle a_{t},u_{t},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},z_{\circ}\rangle),\theta_{0:t}\rangle.

Where:

\displaystyle\theta_{0:t}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\theta_{0:t-1}\oplus\theta_{t}.

\displaystyle\sigma_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t}}(h_{t}\oplus\langle a_{t},u_{t},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},z_{\circ}\rangle)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\Pr(h_{t},a_{t},u_{t},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},z_{\circ}\mid\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t})

\displaystyle=\sum_{s,s^{\prime}\in S}\Pr(h_{t},a_{t},u_{t},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},z_{\circ},s,s^{\prime}\mid\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t})

\displaystyle=\sum_{s,s^{\prime}\in S}\Pr(z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},z_{\circ}\mid h_{t},a_{t},u_{t},s,s^{\prime},\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t})\Pr(h_{t},a_{t},u_{t},s,s^{\prime}\mid\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t}).

The chance of an observation only depends on the state:

\displaystyle=\sum_{s,s^{\prime}\in S}\Pr(z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},z_{\circ}\mid s^{\prime})\Pr(h_{t},a_{t},u_{t},s,s^{\prime}\mid\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t})

\displaystyle=\sum_{s,s^{\prime}\in S}\Pr(z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},z_{\circ}\mid s^{\prime})\Pr(s^{\prime}\mid h_{t},a_{t},u_{t},s,\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t})\Pr(h_{t},a_{t},u_{t},s\mid\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t}).

The chance of reaching a state only depends on the previous state and the agent and nature actions:

\displaystyle=\sum_{s,s^{\prime}\in S}\Pr(z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},z_{\circ}\mid s^{\prime})\Pr(s^{\prime}\mid a_{t},u_{t},s)\Pr(h_{t},a_{t},u_{t},s\mid\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t})

\displaystyle=\sum_{s,s^{\prime}\in S}\Pr(z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},z_{\circ}\mid s^{\prime})\Pr(s^{\prime}\mid a_{t},u_{t},s)\Pr(u_{t}\mid h_{t},a_{t},s,\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t})\Pr(h_{t},a_{t},s\mid\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t}).

The chance of a nature action only depends on nature’s policy at time
t
, the history, and the agent action at time
t
:

\displaystyle=\sum_{s,s^{\prime}\in S}\Pr(z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},z_{\circ}\mid s^{\prime})\Pr(s^{\prime}\mid a_{t},u_{t},s)\Pr(u_{t}\mid h_{t},a_{t},\theta_{t})\Pr(h_{t},a_{t},s\mid\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t})

\displaystyle=\sum_{s,s^{\prime}\in S}\Pr(z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},z_{\circ}\mid s^{\prime})\Pr(s^{\prime}\mid a_{t},u_{t},s)\Pr(u_{t}\mid h_{t},a_{t},\theta_{t})\Pr(a_{t}\mid h_{t},s,\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t})\Pr(h_{t},s\mid\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t}).

The chance of an agent action only depends on the agent’s policy at time
t
, and the history:

\displaystyle=\sum_{s,s^{\prime}\in S}\Pr(z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},z_{\circ}\mid s^{\prime})\Pr(s^{\prime}\mid a_{t},u_{t},s)\Pr(u_{t}\mid h_{t},a_{t},\theta_{t})\Pr(a_{t}\mid h_{t},\pi_{t})\Pr(h_{t},s\mid\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t})

\displaystyle=\sum_{s,s^{\prime}\in S}\Pr(z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},z_{\circ}\mid s^{\prime})\Pr(s^{\prime}\mid a_{t},u_{t},s)\Pr(u_{t}\mid h_{t},a_{t},\theta_{t})\Pr(a_{t}\mid h_{t},\pi_{t})\Pr(s\mid h_{t},\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t})\Pr(h_{t}\mid\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t}).

The chance of being in a state can be computed via the belief generated by the joint history (see
Section

A.2
):

\displaystyle=\sum_{s,s^{\prime}\in S}\Pr(z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},z_{\circ}\mid s^{\prime})\Pr(s^{\prime}\mid a_{t},u_{t},s)\Pr(u_{t}\mid h_{t},a_{t},\theta_{t})\Pr(a_{t}\mid h_{t},\pi_{t})\Pr(s\mid h_{t})\Pr(h_{t}\mid\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t}).

The chance of a history at time
t
does not depend on actions of time
t
:

\displaystyle=\sum_{s,s^{\prime}\in S}\Pr(z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},z_{\circ}\mid s^{\prime})\Pr(s^{\prime}\mid a_{t},u_{t},s)\Pr(u_{t}\mid h_{t},a_{t},\theta_{t})\Pr(a_{t}\mid h_{t},\pi_{t})\Pr(s\mid h_{t})\Pr(h_{t}\mid\pi_{0:t-1},\theta_{0:t-1})

\displaystyle=\sum_{s,s^{\prime}\in S}O^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet}(s^{\prime},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}})O^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet}(s^{\prime},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}})O_{\circ}(s^{\prime},z_{\circ})\Pr(s^{\prime}\mid a_{t},u_{t},s)\Pr(u_{t}\mid h_{t},a_{t},\theta_{t})\Pr(a_{t}\mid h_{t},\pi_{t})\Pr(s\mid h_{t})\Pr(h_{t}\mid\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t})

\displaystyle=\sum_{s,s^{\prime}\in S}O^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet}(s^{\prime},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}})O^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet}(s^{\prime},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}})O_{\circ}(s^{\prime},z_{\circ})\bm{T}(u_{t})(s,a_{t})(s^{\prime})\Pr(u_{t}\mid h_{t},a_{t},\theta_{t})\Pr(a_{t}\mid h_{t},\pi_{t})\Pr(s\mid h_{t})\Pr(h_{t}\mid\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t})

\displaystyle=\sum_{s,s^{\prime}\in S}O^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet}(s^{\prime},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}})O^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet}(s^{\prime},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}})O_{\circ}(s^{\prime},z_{\circ})\bm{T}(u_{t})(s,a_{t})(s^{\prime})\theta_{t}(h^{\mathfrak{n}}_{t},a_{t})(u_{t})\Pr(a_{t}\mid h_{t},\pi_{t})\Pr(s\mid h_{t})\Pr(h_{t}\mid\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t})
