\displaystyle=\sum_{s,s^{\prime}\in S}O^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet}(s^{\prime},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}})O^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet}(s^{\prime},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}})O_{\circ}(s^{\prime},z_{\circ})\bm{T}(u_{t})(s,a_{t})(s^{\prime})\theta_{t}(h^{\mathfrak{n}}_{t},a_{t})(u_{t})\pi_{t}(h^{\mathfrak{a}}_{t})(a_{t})\Pr(s\mid h_{t})\Pr(h_{t}\mid\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t})

\displaystyle=\sum_{s,s^{\prime}\in S}O^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet}(s^{\prime},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}})O^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet}(s^{\prime},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}})O_{\circ}(s^{\prime},z_{\circ})\bm{T}(u_{t})(s,a_{t})(s^{\prime})\theta_{t}(h^{\mathfrak{n}}_{t},a_{t})(u_{t})\pi_{t}(h^{\mathfrak{a}}_{t})(a_{t})b(s,h_{t})\Pr(h_{t}\mid\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t}).

Where
b(s,h_{t})
is the belief computed by
t
belief updates given the joint history
h_{t}
(see
Section

A.2
).

\displaystyle=\sum_{s,s^{\prime}\in S}O^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet}(s^{\prime},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}})O^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet}(s^{\prime},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}})O_{\circ}(s^{\prime},z_{\circ})\bm{T}(u_{t})(s,a_{t})(s^{\prime})\theta_{t}(h^{\mathfrak{n}}_{t},a_{t})(u_{t})\pi_{t}(h^{\mathfrak{a}}_{t})(a_{t})b(s,h_{t})\sigma_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t-1}}(h_{t}).

This shows that we can compute the successor occupancy state using only the previous occupancy state
\text{OS}_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t-1}}=\langle\sigma_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t-1}},\theta_{0:t-1}\rangle
and policies
\pi_{t},\theta_{t}
at time
t
.
Note that we can use the nature policy
\theta_{0:t}
to generate the finite subset of relevant histories
\mathsf{rel}(\theta_{0:t})\subset H
that possibly have a non-zero probability.
We can then select the relevant histories of
t
time steps, denoted as
\mathsf{rel}(\theta_{0:t})_{t}\subset H_{t}
, to compute the occupancy states.
See
Section

A.2
for details on the set of relevant histories.

Next, we look at the expected reward.

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[r_{t}\mid\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t}]

\displaystyle=\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{a\in A}R(s,a)\Pr(s,a\mid\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t})

\displaystyle=\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{a\in A}R(s,a)\sum_{h_{t}\in\mathsf{rel}(\theta_{0:t-1})_{t}}\Pr(s,a,h_{t}\mid\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t})

\displaystyle=\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{a\in A}R(s,a)\sum_{h_{t}\in\mathsf{rel}(\theta_{0:t-1})_{t}}\Pr(a\mid s,h_{t},\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t})\Pr(s,h_{t}\mid\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t}).

The chance of an agent action only depends on the agents’s policy at time
t
, and the history:

\displaystyle=\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{a\in A}R(s,a)\sum_{h_{t}\in\mathsf{rel}(\theta_{0:t-1})_{t}}\Pr(a\mid h_{t},\pi_{t})\Pr(s,h_{t}\mid\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t})

\displaystyle=\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{a\in A}R(s,a)\sum_{h_{t}\in\mathsf{rel}(\theta_{0:t-1})_{t}}\Pr(a\mid h_{t},\pi_{t})\Pr(s\mid h_{t},\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t})\Pr(h_{t}\mid\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t}).

The chance of being in a state can be computed via the belief generated by the joint history (see
Section

A.2
):

\displaystyle=\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{a\in A}R(s,a)\sum_{h_{t}\in\mathsf{rel}(\theta_{0:t-1})_{t}}\Pr(a\mid h_{t},\pi_{t})\Pr(s\mid h_{t})\Pr(h_{t}\mid\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t}).

The chance of a history at time
t
does not depend on actions of time
t
:

\displaystyle=\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{a\in A}R(s,a)\sum_{h_{t}\in\mathsf{rel}(\theta_{0:t-1})_{t}}\Pr(a\mid h_{t},\pi_{t})\Pr(s\mid h_{t})\Pr(h_{t}\mid\pi_{0:t-1},\theta_{0:t-1})

\displaystyle=\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{a\in A}R(s,a)\sum_{h_{t}\in\mathsf{rel}(\theta_{0:t-1})_{t}}\pi_{t}(h^{\mathfrak{a}}_{t})(a)\Pr(s\mid h_{t})\Pr(h_{t}\mid\pi_{0:t-1},\theta_{0:t-1})

\displaystyle=\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{a\in A}R(s,a)\sum_{h_{t}\in\mathsf{rel}(\theta_{0:t-1})_{t}}\pi_{t}(h^{\mathfrak{a}}_{t})(a)b(s,h_{t})\Pr(h_{t}\mid\pi_{0:t-1},\theta_{0:t-1})

\displaystyle=\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{a\in A}R(s,a)\sum_{h_{t}\in\mathsf{rel}(\theta_{0:t-1})_{t}}\pi_{t}(h^{\mathfrak{a}}_{t})(a)b(s,h_{t})\sigma_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t-1}}(h_{t}).

This shows that we can compute the expected reward at time
t
using only the previous occupancy state
\text{OS}_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t-1}}=(\sigma_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t-1}},\theta_{0:t-1})
and policy
\pi_{t}
at time
t
.

Remark 5
.

The equivalent formulation of the occupancy state using POSG notation is as follows:

\displaystyle\text{OS}_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t}}(h_{t}\oplus\langle\langle z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}},z_{\circ}\rangle,\langle z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},z_{\circ},\bot\rangle,a_{t},\langle z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}},z_{\circ}\rangle,\langle z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},z_{\circ},a_{t}\rangle,u_{t}\rangle)

\displaystyle\qquad\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\langle\sigma_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t}}(h_{t}\oplus\langle\langle z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}},z_{\circ}\rangle,\langle z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},z_{\circ},\bot\rangle,a_{t},\langle z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}},z_{\circ}\rangle,\langle z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},z_{\circ},a_{t}\rangle,u_{t}\rangle),\theta_{0:t}\rangle.

Where:

\displaystyle\theta_{0:t}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\theta_{0:t-1}\oplus\theta_{t}.

\displaystyle\sigma_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t}}(h_{t}\oplus\langle\langle z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}},z_{\circ}\rangle,\langle z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},z_{\circ},\bot\rangle,a_{t},\langle z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}},z_{\circ}\rangle,\langle z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},z_{\circ},a_{t}\rangle,u_{t}\rangle)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\Pr(h_{t},a_{t},u_{t},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},z_{\circ}\mid\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t})

\displaystyle=\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{a}}}\sum_{s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{O}^{\mathfrak{a}}(s^{\prime},\langle z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}},z_{\circ}\rangle)\mathcal{O}^{\mathfrak{n}}(s^{\prime},\langle z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},z_{\circ}\rangle)\mathcal{T}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\mathcal{T}^{\mathfrak{a}}(s,a_{t}),u_{t},s^{\prime})\theta_{t}(h^{\mathfrak{n}}_{t},a_{t})(u_{t})\pi_{t}(h^{\mathfrak{a}}_{t})(a_{t})b(s,h_{t})\sigma_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t-1}}(h_{t}).

We can compute the expected reward as follows:

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[r_{t}\mid\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t}]

\displaystyle=\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{a}}}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{R}(s,a)\sum_{h_{t}\in\mathsf{rel}(\theta_{0:t-1})_{t}}\pi_{t}(h^{\mathfrak{a}}_{t})(a)b(s,h_{t})\sigma_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t-1}}(h_{t}).

This formulation again shows that the occupancy state
\text{OS}_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t-1}}
together with agent and nature policies
\pi_{t},\theta_{t}
at time
t
, is a sufficient statistic for computing the next occupancy state
\text{OS}_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t}}
and the expected reward
\mathsf{R}(\text{OS}_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t-1}},\pi_{t},\theta_{t})
.

G.2
Occupancy Game

Given the occupancy state, we can define a non-observable, non-stochastic game: a zero-sum occupancy game (OG)
Delage et al. [2023]
.
As the occupancy state is a sufficient statistic, computing a Nash equilibrium in this OG is equivalent to a Nash equilibrium in our original RPOMDP.

Definition 19

(Occupancy game)
.

Given an RPOMDP
\langle S,A,\bm{T},R,Z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}},Z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},Z_{\circ},O^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},O^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},O_{\circ},\mathsf{stick},{\mathfrak{a}}\rangle
, and a horizon
K\in\mathbb{N}
, we define the occupancy game as a tuple
(\mathsf{S}^{\mathfrak{a}},\mathsf{S}^{\mathfrak{n}},\mathsf{A}^{\mathfrak{a}},\mathsf{A}^{\mathfrak{n}},\mathsf{T},\mathsf{R})
where the sets of states and actions are defined as follows:

\mathsf{S}^{\mathfrak{a}}=\bigcup_{t=0}^{K-1}\bigcup_{\pi_{0:t}\in\Pi_{0:t}}\bigcup_{\theta_{0:t}\in\Theta_{0:t}}\text{OS}_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t}}
is the infinite set of agent states, and
\mathsf{S}^{\mathfrak{n}}=\bigcup_{t=0}^{K-1}(\bigcup_{\pi_{0:t}\in\Pi_{0:t}}\bigcup_{\theta_{0:t}\in\Theta_{0:t}}\text{OS}_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t}}\times\Pi_{t+1})
the infinite set of nature states;

\mathsf{A}^{\mathfrak{a}}=\bigcup_{t=0}^{K-1}\Pi_{t}
is the infinite set of agent actions, and
\mathsf{A}^{\mathfrak{n}}=\bigcup_{t=0}^{K-1}\Theta_{t}
the infinite set of nature actions;
The transition and reward functions are then defined as:

•

\mathsf{T}=\mathsf{T}^{\mathfrak{a}}\cup\mathsf{T}^{\mathfrak{n}}
, the transition function, where:

–

\mathsf{T}^{\mathfrak{a}}\colon\mathsf{S}^{\mathfrak{a}}\times\mathsf{A}^{\mathfrak{a}}\hookrightarrow\mathsf{S}^{\mathfrak{n}}
the agent’s transition function.

–

\mathsf{T}^{\mathfrak{n}}\colon\mathsf{S}^{\mathfrak{n}}\times\mathsf{A}^{\mathfrak{n}}\hookrightarrow\mathsf{S}^{\mathfrak{a}}
nature’s transition function.

•

\mathsf{R}\colon\mathsf{S}^{\mathfrak{a}}\times\mathsf{A}^{\mathfrak{a}}\to\mathbb{R}
the reward function.

Where:

•

\mathsf{R}(\langle\sigma_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t}},\theta_{0:t}\rangle,\pi_{t+1})=\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{a\in A}R(s,a)\sum_{h_{t}\in\mathsf{rel}(\theta_{0:t-1})_{t}}\pi_{t}(h^{\mathfrak{a}}_{t},a)b(s,h_{t})\sigma_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t-1}}(h_{t})
.

•

\mathsf{T^{\mathfrak{a}}}(\langle\sigma_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t}},\theta_{0:t}\rangle,\pi_{t+1})=\langle\langle\sigma_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t}},\theta_{0:t}\rangle,\pi_{t+1}\rangle
.

•

\mathsf{T^{\mathfrak{n}}}(\langle\langle\sigma_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t}},\theta_{0:t}\rangle,\pi_{t+1}\rangle,\theta_{t+1})=\langle\sigma_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t+1}},\theta_{0:t+1}\rangle
, where:

–

\theta_{0:t+1}=\theta_{0:t}\oplus\theta_{t+1}
.

–

\forall h_{t+1}\in\mathsf{rel}(\theta_{0:t})_{t+1},\forall a\in\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{a}},\forall u\in\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{n}},\forall z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\in Z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}}\times Z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}}\times Z_{\circ},\sigma_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t+1}}(\langle h_{t+1},a,u,z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle)=

\sum_{s,s^{\prime}\in S}O^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet}(s^{\prime},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}})O^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet}(s^{\prime},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}})O_{\circ}(s^{\prime},z_{\circ})\bm{T}(u_{t})(s,a_{t})(s^{\prime})\theta_{t}(h^{\mathfrak{n}}_{t},a_{t})(u_{t})\pi_{t}(h^{\mathfrak{a}}_{t})(a_{t})b(s,h_{t})\sigma_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t-1}}(h_{t}).

Where
b(s,h_{t})
is the belief computed by
t
belief updates given the joint history
h_{t}
(see
Section

A.2
).
For deriving the reward and transition functions, see
Section

G.1
.

G.3
Mixed policies

As shown in
Section

G.1
, the occupancy state is a sufficient statistic for the POSG and, hence, for the RPOMDP.
In
section

G.4
, we show that the occupancy game has a Nash equilibrium for finite horizon reward maximization, and an optimal policy for the agent exists.
To prove that this Nash equilibrium exists, we need to reason with mixed policies instead of stochastic policies.
In this section, we prove that reasoning with the set of mixed agent and nature policies results in the same set of distributions over paths, and hence the same possible values, as reasoning with the set of stochastic policies.

Concretely, we need to show that for every stochastic policy, there exists a mixed policy that behaves equivalently, meaning it results in the same distribution over paths.
We focus on the RPOMDP policies.
The same results follow for the POSG policies using the bijections from
Appendix

F
.

Theorem 5

(Existence of equivalent mixed policy)
.

Let
\mu^{\pi,\theta}\in\Delta(\text{Paths}^{M})
be the probability distribution over paths in the RPOMDP resulting from executing agent policy
\pi
and nature policy
\theta
.
Then:

\forall\pi\in\Pi,\exists\pi^{mix}\in\Pi^{mix},\forall\theta\in\Theta\cup\Theta^{mix}.\,\mu^{\pi,\theta}=\mu^{\pi^{mix},\theta},

\forall\theta\in\Theta,\exists\theta^{mix}\in\Theta^{mix},\forall\pi\in\Pi\cup\Pi^{mix}.\,\mu^{\pi,\theta}=\mu^{\pi,\theta^{mix}}.

Before proving the theorem above, we consider the other key results that follow.
We immediately get the following corollary from
Theorem

5
.

Corollary 7

(stochastic policies
\subseteq
mixed policies)
.

Let
\mu^{\pi,\theta}\in\Delta(\text{Paths}^{M})
be the probability distribution over paths in the RPOMDP resulting from executing agent policy
\pi
and nature policy
\theta
.
Then we have the following:

\{\mu^{\pi,\theta}\mid\pi\in\Pi,\theta\in\Theta\}\subseteq\{\mu^{\pi^{mix},\theta^{mix}}\mid\pi^{mix}\in\Pi^{mix},\theta^{mix}\in\Theta^{mix}\}.

We also need to show that for every mixed policy, there exists a stochastic policy that behaves equivalently.
This means that there are no new behaviors, and consequently no new values, introduced by looking at the set of mixed policies.

Theorem 6

(Existence of equivalent stochastic policy)
.

Let
\mu^{\pi,\theta}\in\Delta(\text{Paths}^{M})
be the probability distribution over paths in the RPOMDP resulting from executing agent policy
\pi
and nature policy
\theta
. Then:

\forall\pi^{mix}\in\Pi^{mix},\exists\pi\in\Pi,\forall\theta\in\Theta\cup\Theta^{mix}.\mu^{\pi^{mix},\theta}=\mu^{\pi,\theta},

\forall\theta^{mix}\in\Theta^{mix},\exists\theta\in\Theta,\forall\pi\in\Pi\cup\Pi^{mix}.\,\mu^{\pi,\theta^{mix}}=\mu^{\pi,\theta}.

Theorem

6
comes with the following corollary.

Corollary 8

(stochastic policies
\supseteq
mixed policies)
.

Let
\mu^{\pi,\theta}\in\Delta(\text{Paths}^{M})
be the probability distribution over paths in the RPOMDP resulting from executing agent policy
\pi
and nature policy
\theta
.
Then we have the following:

\{\mu^{\pi,\theta}\mid\pi\in\Pi,\theta\in\Theta\}\supseteq\{\mu^{\pi^{mix},\theta^{mix}}\mid\pi^{mix}\in\Pi^{mix},\theta^{mix}\in\Theta^{mix}\}.

By combining
Corollaries

7
and
8
, it follows that the sets of mixed policies give exactly the same sets of distributions over paths in our original RPOMDP as the sets of stochastic policies do.

Corollary 9

(Equivalent set of mixed policies)
.

Let
\mu^{\pi,\theta}\in\Delta(\text{Paths}^{M})
be the probability distribution over paths in the RPOMDP resulting from executing agent policy
\pi
and nature policy
\theta
.
Then we have the following:

\{\mu^{\pi,\theta}\mid\pi\in\Pi,\theta\in\Theta\}=\{\mu^{\pi^{mix},\theta^{mix}}\mid\pi^{mix}\in\Pi^{mix},\theta^{mix}\in\Theta^{mix}\}.

It follows that the sets of possible values,
i.e.
, the subset of
\mathbb{R}
the value function can attain under all stochastic policies and all mixed policies, is the same:

\{V^{\pi,\theta}\mid\pi\in\Pi,\theta\in\Theta\}=\{V^{\pi^{mix},\theta^{mix}}\mid\pi^{mix}\in\Pi^{mix},\theta^{mix}\in\Theta^{mix}\}.

Below, we first define some definitions and lemmas and then prove
Theorems

5
and
6
.
We focus on the nature policies, as these require dealing with an infinite action space and, therefore, with an infinite set of deterministic policies.
The proofs for the agent policies follow the same steps.

Additional definitions and lemmas

We begin by defining the set of relevant histories given a policy.
The actions chosen for histories outside the relevant history set do not influence the results of a game since the policy never reaches them.

Using the relevant histories, we can define the set of relevant deterministic policies given a history.

Definition 20

(Relevant deterministic policies)
.

Given a history
h^{\mathfrak{n}}\in H^{\mathfrak{n}}
, we define the set of relevant deterministic policies
\Theta^{{det},h}
, containing all deterministic policies that could have generated the current history.

\Theta^{{det},h^{\mathfrak{n}}}=\{\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{det}\mid h^{\mathfrak{n}}\in\mathsf{rel}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\theta^{det})\}.

We define a helper function
\eta^{\pi,\theta}\colon\Delta(\text{Paths}^{M})
to compute the probability over paths for all stochastic and deterministic policies
\pi\in\Pi
and
\theta\in\Theta
:

\displaystyle\eta^{\pi,\theta}(\langle s_{I}\rangle)

\displaystyle=1,

\displaystyle\eta^{\pi,\theta}(\tau^{\prime}\oplus\langle s,a,u,s^{\prime}\rangle)

\displaystyle=\eta^{\pi,\theta}(\tau^{\prime}\oplus\langle s\rangle)\cdot\pi(O^{{\mathfrak{a}},M}(\tau^{\prime}\oplus\langle s\rangle))(a)\cdot\theta(O^{{\mathfrak{n}},M}(\tau^{\prime}\oplus\langle s\rangle),a)(u)\cdot\bm{T}(u)(s,a,s^{\prime}).

We now prove the following lemmas about the probability distribution over paths for deterministic policies.

Given a path, if a deterministic policy is not relevant for generating the history of that path, then the probability of reaching that path with the deterministic policy is zero.

Lemma 5

(Zero probability of non-relevant paths)
.

Given a path
\tau
and policies
\pi\in\Pi
,
\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{det}
, we have that:

\theta^{det}\notin\Theta^{{det},O^{{\mathfrak{n}},M}(\tau)}\implies\eta^{\pi,\theta^{det}}(\tau)=0.

Proof.

Take arbitrary path
\tau
and policies
\pi\in\Pi
,
\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{det}
.

\theta^{det}\notin\Theta^{{det},O^{{\mathfrak{n}},M}(\tau)}\iff O^{{\mathfrak{n}},M}(\tau)\notin\mathsf{rel}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\theta^{det}).

By definition, we know that
O^{{\mathfrak{n}},M}(\langle s_{I}\rangle)\in\mathsf{rel}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\theta^{det})
.
Furthermore, we know that:

O^{{\mathfrak{n}},M}(\tau^{\prime}\oplus\langle a^{\prime},u^{\prime},s\rangle)\notin\mathsf{rel}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\theta^{det})\iff\theta^{det}(O^{{\mathfrak{n}},M}(\tau^{\prime}),a^{\prime})\neq u^{\prime}\lor O^{{\mathfrak{n}},M}(\tau^{\prime})\notin\mathsf{rel}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\theta^{det}).

Since
O^{{\mathfrak{n}},M}(\langle s_{I}\rangle)\in\mathsf{rel}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\theta^{det})
, we will eventually reach a prefix of
\tau
, for which the condition is violated. So then we get:

\displaystyle O^{{\mathfrak{n}},M}(\tau)\notin\mathsf{rel}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\theta^{det})

\displaystyle\iff\exists\tau^{\prime\prime}.\,\tau^{\prime\prime}\oplus\langle a^{\prime\prime},u^{\prime\prime},s^{\prime},\dots\rangle=\tau\land\theta^{det}(O^{{\mathfrak{n}},M}(\tau^{\prime\prime}),a^{\prime\prime})\neq u^{\prime\prime}

\displaystyle\iff\exists\tau^{\prime\prime}.\,\tau^{\prime\prime}\oplus\langle a^{\prime\prime},u^{\prime\prime},s^{\prime},\dots\rangle=\tau\land\theta^{det}(O^{{\mathfrak{n}},M}(\tau^{\prime\prime}),a^{\prime\prime})(u^{\prime\prime})=0

\displaystyle\>\implies\exists\tau^{\prime\prime}.\,\tau^{\prime\prime}\oplus\langle a^{\prime\prime},u^{\prime\prime},s^{\prime},\dots\rangle=\tau\land\eta^{\pi,\theta^{det}}(\tau^{\prime\prime}\oplus\langle a^{\prime\prime},u^{\prime\prime},s^{\prime}\rangle)=0

\displaystyle\>\implies\eta^{\pi,\theta^{det}}(\tau)=0.

Hence:

\theta^{det}\notin\Theta^{{det},O^{{\mathfrak{n}},M}(\tau)}\implies\eta^{\pi,\theta^{det}}(\tau)=0.

∎

The next lemma states that, given a path, if two deterministic policies are both relevant for generating the history of that path, then the probability of reaching that path is the same for both policies.

Lemma 6

(Constant probability of paths for relevant deterministic policies)
.

Given a path
\tau
and policy
\pi\in\Pi
, we have that:

\forall\theta^{det},\theta^{{det}^{\prime}}\in\Theta^{{det},O^{{\mathfrak{n}},M}(\tau)}.\,\eta^{\pi,\theta^{det}}(\tau)=\eta^{\pi,\theta^{{det}^{\prime}}}(\tau).

Proof.

Take arbitrary path
\tau
, policy
\pi\in\Pi
and
\theta^{det},\theta^{{det}^{\prime}}\in\Theta^{{det},O^{{\mathfrak{n}},M}(\tau)}
.
We show
\eta^{\pi,\theta^{det}}(\tau)=\eta^{\pi,\theta^{{det}^{\prime}}}(\tau)
by induction on the length of
\tau
.

Assume
|\tau|=0
.
Then
\tau=\langle s_{I}\rangle
.
Then:

\eta^{\pi,\theta^{det}}(\langle s_{I}\rangle)=1=\eta^{\pi,\theta^{{det}^{\prime}}}(\langle s_{I}\rangle).

So for paths
\tau
of length
0
, we know that
\eta^{\pi,\theta^{det}}(\tau)=\eta^{\pi,\theta^{{det}^{\prime}}}(\tau)
.

Now assume we know, given
q\in\mathbb{N},q\geq 1
, that:

\forall\tau\in\text{Paths}^{M}.|\tau|=q-1\implies\eta^{\pi,\theta^{det}}(\tau)=\eta^{\pi,\theta^{{det}^{\prime}}}(\tau).

Take arbitrary
\tau\in\text{Paths}^{M}
with horizon length
|\tau|=q
.
Then we have:

\tau=\tau_{0:q-1}\oplus\langle a_{q-1},u_{q-1},s_{q}\rangle=\tau_{0:q-2}\oplus\langle a_{q-2},u_{q-2},s_{q-1},a_{q-1},u_{q-1},s_{q}\rangle.

Then
\tau_{0:q-1}\in\text{Paths}^{M}
and
|\tau_{0:q-1}|=q-1
.
By assumption, we get that:

\eta^{\pi,\theta^{det}}(\tau_{0:q-1})=\eta^{\pi,\theta^{{det}^{\prime}}}(\tau_{0:q-1}).

Additionally, we know that:

\displaystyle\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{{det},O^{{\mathfrak{n}},M}(\tau)}

\displaystyle\iff O^{{\mathfrak{n}},M}(\tau)\in\mathsf{rel}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\theta^{det})

\displaystyle\iff\theta^{det}(O^{{\mathfrak{n}},M}(\tau_{0:q-1}),a_{q-1})=u_{q-1}\land O^{{\mathfrak{n}},M}(\tau_{0:q-1})\in\mathsf{rel}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\theta^{det})

\displaystyle\iff\theta^{det}(O^{{\mathfrak{n}},M}(\tau_{0:q-1}),a_{q-1})(u_{q-1})=1\land O^{{\mathfrak{n}},M}(\tau_{0:q-1})\in\mathsf{rel}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\theta^{det}).

So we have that:

\theta^{det}(O^{{\mathfrak{n}},M}(\tau_{0:q-1}),a_{q-1})(u_{q-1})=1=\theta^{{det}^{\prime}}(O^{{\mathfrak{n}},M}(\tau_{0:q-1}),a_{q-1})(u_{q-1}).

Finally, we get:

\displaystyle\eta^{\pi,\theta^{det}}(\tau)

\displaystyle=\eta^{\pi,\theta^{det}}(\tau_{0:q-1})\cdot\pi(O^{{\mathfrak{a}},M}(\tau_{0:q-1}))(a_{q-1})\cdot\theta^{det}(O^{{\mathfrak{n}},M}(\tau_{0:q-1}),a_{q-1})(u_{q-1})\cdot\bm{T}(u_{q-1})(s_{q-1},a_{q-1},s_{q})

\displaystyle=\eta^{\pi,\theta^{{det}^{\prime}}}(\tau_{0:q-1})\cdot\pi(O^{{\mathfrak{a}},M}(\tau_{0:q-1}))(a_{q-1})\cdot\theta^{{det}^{\prime}}(O^{{\mathfrak{n}},M}(\tau_{0:q-1}),a_{q-1})(u_{q-1})\cdot\bm{T}(u_{q-1})(s_{q-1},a_{q-1},s_{q})

\displaystyle=\eta^{\pi,\theta^{{det}^{\prime}}}(\tau).

So, if
\eta^{\pi,\theta^{det}}(\tau)=\eta^{\pi,\theta^{{det}^{\prime}}}(\tau)
holds for paths of arbitrary length
q-1\in\mathbb{N}
, then
\eta^{\pi,\theta^{det}}(\tau)=\eta^{\pi,\theta^{{det}^{\prime}}}(\tau)
holds for paths of length
q
.
Hence, by induction,
\eta^{\pi,\theta^{det}}(\tau)=\eta^{\pi,\theta^{{det}^{\prime}}}(\tau)
.

As
\theta^{det},\theta^{{det}^{\prime}}\in\Theta^{{det},O^{{\mathfrak{n}},M}(\tau)}
were arbitrarily chosen, we conclude that:

\forall\theta^{det},\theta^{{det}^{\prime}}\in\Theta^{{det},O^{{\mathfrak{n}},M}(\tau)}.\,\eta^{\pi,\theta^{det}}(\tau)=\eta^{\pi,\theta^{{det}^{\prime}}}(\tau).

∎

Using our helper function
\eta
, we can define the four ways of computing the probability distribution over paths depending on the type of policies involved as follows:

(1)
\pi\in\Pi
and
\theta\in\Theta
:

\displaystyle\mu^{\pi,\theta}(\tau)

\displaystyle=\eta^{\pi,\theta}(\tau).

(2)
\pi\in\Pi
and
\theta^{mix}\in\Theta^{mix}
:

\displaystyle\mu^{\pi,\theta^{mix}}(\tau)

\displaystyle=\sum_{\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{det}}\theta^{mix}(\theta^{det})\cdot\eta^{\pi,\theta^{det}}(\tau).

(3)
\pi^{mix}\in\Pi^{mix}
and
\theta\in\Theta
:

\displaystyle\mu^{\pi^{mix},\theta}(\tau)

\displaystyle=\sum_{\pi^{det}\in\Pi^{det}}\pi^{mix}(\pi^{det})\cdot\eta^{\pi^{det},\theta}(\tau).

(4)
\pi^{mix}\in\Pi^{mix}
and
\theta^{mix}\in\Theta^{mix}
:

\displaystyle\mu^{\pi^{mix},\theta^{mix}}(\tau)

\displaystyle=\sum_{\pi^{det}\in\Pi^{det}}\pi^{mix}(\pi^{det})\cdot\sum_{\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{det}}\theta^{mix}(\theta^{det})\cdot\eta^{\pi^{det},\theta^{det}}(\tau),

\displaystyle=\sum_{\pi^{det}\in\Pi^{det}}\sum_{\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{det}}\pi^{mix}(\pi^{det})\cdot\theta^{mix}(\theta^{det})\cdot\eta^{\pi^{det},\theta^{det}}(\tau).

Recall that a deterministic policy can be interpreted as both a stochastic and a mixed policy using only Dirac distributions.
The probabilities over paths generated by deterministic policies can, therefore, be computed using any of the above formulas.

Proof of
Theorem

5

The standard way to define a mixed strategy given a stochastic strategy is to simply assign to each deterministic policy the product of the probabilities the stochastic policy assigns to the same choices
Kuhn [1953]
.
The problem in our case, however, is that, due to the infinite number of nature policies, this leads to infinitely many deterministic policies having a non-zero probability in the resulting mixed policy.

To create a mixed policy with a finite number of deterministic policies with a non-zero probability, we define an equivalence class for deterministic policies that assign the same action for all histories that are relevant to the given stochastic policy.

Definition 21
.

Given a stochastic policy
\theta\in\Theta
, we define the following equivalence relation
{\sim_{\mathsf{rel}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\theta)}}
between deterministic policies, which we call
\mathsf{rel}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\theta)
-equivalent:

\forall\theta^{det},\theta^{{det}^{\prime}}\in\Theta^{det}.\,\theta^{det}{\sim_{\mathsf{rel}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\theta)}}\theta^{{det}^{\prime}}\iff\forall h^{\mathfrak{n}}\in\mathsf{rel}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\theta),\forall a\in A.\,\theta^{det}(h^{\mathfrak{n}},a)=\theta^{{det}^{\prime}}(h^{\mathfrak{n}},a).

The reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity of the
\mathsf{rel}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\theta)
-equivalence relation follow from the reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity of the equality relation.

The
\mathsf{rel}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\theta)
-equivalence relation provides us with
\mathsf{rel}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\theta)
-equivalence classes
[\theta^{det}]_{\sim_{\mathsf{rel}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\theta)}}
, which partition the set of deterministic policies.
We select one member of each
\mathsf{rel}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\theta)
-equivalence class to define a new set
\theta^{{det},{\sim_{\mathsf{rel}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\theta)}}}
called the
\mathsf{rel}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\theta)
-representation set.
Note that this set is not the same as the quotient set
\Theta^{det}/{\sim_{\mathsf{rel}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\theta)}}
, as the quotient set is a set of sets of deterministic policies, whereas the
\mathsf{rel}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\theta)
-representation set is a set of deterministic policies.
Clearly,
\Theta^{det}/{\sim_{\mathsf{rel}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\theta)}}\subseteq\Theta^{det}
.

Using the
\mathsf{rel}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\theta)
-representation set, we define a function
g\colon\Theta\to\Theta^{mix}
with which we will construct our equivalent mixed policy.
This function uses a similar construction as in
Kuhn [1953]
for the deterministic policies in the
\mathsf{rel}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\theta)
-representation set but gives the rest of the deterministic policies a zero probability automatically.

g(\theta)(\theta^{det})=\begin{cases}\prod_{h^{\mathfrak{n}}\in\mathsf{rel}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\theta),a\in A}\theta(h,a)(\theta^{det}(h^{\mathfrak{n}},a))&\text{ if }\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{{det},{\sim_{\mathsf{rel}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\theta)}}},\\
0&\text{ otherwise.}\end{cases}

We first show that
g
correctly maps to a mixed policy (
Lemma

7
) and then that this resulting policy results in the same distribution over paths in the RPOMDP given any agent policy (
Lemma

8
).

Lemma 7
.

g(\theta)
is a mixed policy:

\forall\theta\in\Theta.\,g(\theta)\in\Theta^{mix}.

Proof.

Take arbitrary
\theta\in\Theta
.
By construction, we have that
g(\theta)\colon\Theta^{det}\to[0,1]
.
Now to show that
g(\theta)\in\Theta^{mix}
, we must show two things:
g(\theta)
assigns a non-zero probability to a finite number of deterministic policies (finitely randomizing) and
g(\theta)
is a probability distribution, meaning the probabilities sum up to
1
.

\displaystyle g(\theta)\text{ is finitely randomizing},

(2)

\displaystyle\sum_{\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{det}}g(\theta)(\theta^{det})=1.

(3)

When proving
Equation

2
, we can restrict ourselves to
\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{{det},{\sim_{\mathsf{rel}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\theta)}}}
, as we assign a zero probability to all other deterministic policies.
There can be infinitely many
\mathsf{rel}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\theta)
-equivalence classes and, therefore, infinitely many elements of
\Theta^{{det},{\sim_{\mathsf{rel}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\theta)}}}
.
However, we know that there is a finite number of nature histories in
\mathsf{rel}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\theta)
since
\theta
is finitely randomizing,
Z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},Z_{\circ}
, and
A
are finite, and we consider a finite horizon.
Furthermore, we know that because
\theta
is finitely randomizing, there are only finitely many
u
that can be chosen by the deterministic policies at each history action pair
h^{\mathfrak{n}},a
for which
\theta(h^{\mathfrak{n}},a)(u)
gives a non-zero probability.
Due to the
\mathsf{rel}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\theta)
-equivalence classes, we only have one deterministic policy per unique choice combination for all relevant histories.
Combining this with the fact that there are a finite number of choices that give a non-zero probability, we can conclude that there is a finite number of deterministic policies that give a non-zero probability.

Equation

3
follows from the fact that, by construction, there is exactly one deterministic policy with a non-zero probability for each choice combination of choices available in the stochastic policies over all relevant nature histories of that stochastic policy.
Each of these deterministic policies is assigned the product of the probabilities assigned to the same choices by the stochastic policy for the relevant nature histories.
Summing over the deterministic policies will hence equal summing over the product of the probabilities assigned to the choices by the stochastic policy for the relevant nature histories.
Since the stochastic policy assigns a probability distribution over its choices for each relevant nature history, we also get that:

\sum_{\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{det}}g(\theta)(\theta^{det})=1.

∎

The following lemma is the last but vital ingredient towards the proof of
Theorem

5
.

g(\theta)

Proof of
Theorem

6

We define a function
f\colon\Theta^{mix}\to\Theta
with which we will construct our equivalent stochastic policy.
This function follows the construction used in
Kuhn [1953]
.
Note that we cannot directly apply Kuhn’s theorem, as our game is not finite.
If a nature history is relevant for the mixed policy, the probability for each choice in the resulting stochastic policy will only take the probability of deterministic policies that can reach that nature history into account.
Nature histories that are not relevant for the mixed policy will also not be relevant for the resulting policy, so for those histories, we can just look at the probability of all deterministic policies.

f(\theta^{mix})(h^{\mathfrak{n}},a)(u)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{\sum_{\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{{det},h^{\mathfrak{n}}}}\theta^{det}(h^{\mathfrak{n}},a)(u)\cdot\theta^{mix}(\theta^{det})}{\sum_{\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{{det},h^{\mathfrak{n}}}}\theta^{mix}(\theta^{det})}&\text{ if }h^{\mathfrak{n}}\in\mathsf{rel}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\theta^{mix}),\\[14.22636pt]
\sum_{\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{det}}\theta^{det}(h^{\mathfrak{n}},a)(u)\cdot\theta^{mix}(\theta^{det})&\text{ if }h^{\mathfrak{n}}\not\in\mathsf{rel}^{\mathfrak{n}}(\theta^{mix}).\end{cases}

where

\displaystyle\theta^{det}(h^{\mathfrak{n}},a)(u)

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}1&\text{ if }\theta^{det}(h^{\mathfrak{n}},a)=u,\\
0&\text{ otherwise}.\end{cases}

We first show that
f
correctly maps to a stochastic policy (
Lemma

9
) and then that this resulting policy results in the same distribution over paths in the RPOMDP given any agent policy (
Lemma

10
).

Lemma 9

(
f(\theta^{mix})
is a stochastic policy)
.

\forall\theta^{mix}\in\Theta^{mix}.\,f(\theta^{mix})\in\Theta.

Proof.

Take arbitrary
\theta^{mix}\in\Theta^{mix}
.
By construction, we have that
f(\theta^{mix})\in H^{\mathfrak{n}}\times A\to\Delta(\bm{U})
.
Now to show that
f(\theta^{mix})\in\Theta
, we must show two things:
f(\theta^{mix})
assigns a non-zero probability to a finite number of variable assignments (finitely randomizing) and
f(\theta^{mix})
is valid, meaning it adheres to the stickiness restrictions (see
Section

3.1
).

\displaystyle\forall h^{\mathfrak{n}}\in H^{\mathfrak{n}},\forall a\in A.f(\theta^{mix})(h^{\mathfrak{n}},a)\text{ is finitely randomizing},

(4)

\displaystyle\forall h^{\mathfrak{n}}\in H^{\mathfrak{n}},\forall a\in A,\forall u\in f(\theta^{mix})(h^{\mathfrak{n}},a).u\in\bm{U}^{\mathcal{P}}(\mathsf{fix}(h^{\mathfrak{n}})).

(5)

Equation

4
follows from
\theta^{mix}
being finitely randomizing by definition.
Every choice in
f(\theta^{mix})
assigns a non-zero probability to a number of variable assignments less than or equal to the number of the deterministic policies with a non-zero probability in the mixed policy.
As this number of deterministic policies is finite, the resulting policy
f(\theta^{mix})
is finitely randomizing.

Equation

5
follows from the fact that the deterministic policies used to construct
f(\theta^{mix})
are valid policies by definition, so we have

\forall\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{det},\forall h^{\mathfrak{n}}\in H^{\mathfrak{n}},\forall a\in A,\theta^{det}(h^{\mathfrak{n}},a)\in\bm{U}^{\mathcal{P}}(\mathsf{fix}(h^{\mathfrak{n}})).

Combining this with the fact that

\forall h^{\mathfrak{n}}\in H^{\mathfrak{n}},\forall a\in A,\forall u\in f(\theta^{mix})(h^{\mathfrak{n}},a),\exists\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{det}.\,\theta^{mix}(\theta^{det})>0\land\theta^{det}(h^{\mathfrak{n}},a)=u,

gives us the desired result:

\forall h^{\mathfrak{n}}\in H^{\mathfrak{n}},\forall a\in A,\forall u\in f(\theta^{mix})(h^{\mathfrak{n}},a).u\in\bm{U}^{\mathcal{P}}(\mathsf{fix}(h^{\mathfrak{n}})).

∎

Lemma 10
.

f(\theta^{mix})
equivalent to
\theta^{mix}
:

\forall\theta^{mix}\in\Theta^{mix},\forall\pi\in\Pi\cup\Pi^{mix}.\,\mu^{\pi,\theta^{mix}}=\mu^{\pi,f(\theta^{mix})}.

Proof.

Take arbitrary
\theta^{mix}\in\Theta^{mix}
.
We show
\forall\pi\in\Pi\cup\Pi^{mix},\forall\tau\in\text{Paths}^{M}.\,\mu^{\pi,\theta^{mix}}(\tau)=\mu^{\pi,f(\theta^{mix})}(\tau)
by induction on the length of the path
\tau
.
We write the length of
\tau
as
|\tau|
.

Assume
|\tau|=0
.
Then
\tau=\langle s_{I}\rangle
.
Then we have for
\pi\in\Pi

\displaystyle\mu^{\pi,\theta^{mix}}(\langle s_{I}\rangle)

\displaystyle=\sum_{\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{det}}\theta^{mix}(\theta^{det})\cdot\eta^{\pi,\theta^{det}}(\langle s_{I}\rangle)

\displaystyle=\sum_{\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{det}}\theta^{mix}(\theta^{det})\cdot 1

\displaystyle=1

\displaystyle=\eta^{\pi,f(\theta^{mix})}(\langle s_{I}\rangle)

\displaystyle=\mu^{\pi,f(\theta^{mix})}(\langle s_{I}\rangle),

and for
\pi^{mix}\in\Pi^{mix}

\displaystyle\mu^{\pi^{mix},\theta^{mix}}(\langle s_{I}\rangle)

\displaystyle=\sum_{\pi^{det}\in\Pi^{det}}\pi^{mix}(\pi^{det})\cdot\sum_{\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{det}}\theta^{mix}(\theta^{det})\cdot\eta^{\pi,\theta^{det}}(\langle s_{I}\rangle)

\displaystyle=\sum_{\pi^{det}\in\Pi^{det}}\pi^{mix}(\pi^{det})\cdot\sum_{\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{det}}\theta^{mix}(\theta^{det})\cdot 1

\displaystyle=\sum_{\pi^{det}\in\Pi^{det}}\pi^{mix}(\pi^{det})\cdot 1

\displaystyle=\sum_{\pi^{det}\in\Pi^{det}}\pi^{mix}(\pi^{det})\cdot\eta^{\pi,f(\theta^{mix})}(\langle s_{I}\rangle)

\displaystyle=\mu^{\pi^{mix},f(\theta^{mix})}(\langle s_{I}\rangle).

So for paths

of length 0, we know that
\forall\pi\in\Pi\cup\Pi^{mix}.\,\mu^{\pi,\theta^{mix}}(\tau)=\mu^{\pi,f(\theta^{mix})}(\tau)
.

Now assume we know, given

\forall\tau\in\text{Paths}^{M}.|\tau|=q-1\implies\forall\pi\in\Pi\cup\Pi^{mix}.\,\mu^{\pi,\theta^{mix}}(\tau)=\mu^{\pi,f(\theta^{mix})}(\tau).

Take arbitrary

By assumption, we get that:

\displaystyle=\mu^{\pi^{mix},f(\theta^{mix})}(\tau).

We can now prove the nature case of
Theorem

6
:
See
6

Proof.

Take arbitrary
\theta^{mix}\in\Theta^{mix}
.
By
Lemma

9
, we know that:

f(\theta^{mix})\in\Theta.

Furthermore, by
Lemma

10
, we know that:

\forall\pi\in\Pi\cup\Pi^{mix}.\,\mu^{\pi,\theta^{mix}}=\mu^{\pi,f(\theta^{mix})}.

Hence, we know that:

\exists\theta\in\Theta,\forall\pi\in\Pi\cup\Pi^{mix}.\,\mu^{\pi,\theta^{mix}}=\mu^{\pi,\theta}.

As

was arbitrarily chosen, we conclude that:

\forall\theta^{mix}\in\Theta^{mix},\exists\theta\in\Theta,\forall\pi\in\Pi\cup\Pi^{mix}.\,\mu^{\pi,\theta^{mix}}=\mu^{\pi,\theta}.

∎

G.4
Convex Semi-Infinite Game

Although we follow the occupancy game construction from
Delage et al. [2023]
, their proof for Nash equilibrium existence requires both players to have convex subsets of a Euclidean space as their policy space.
Our set of nature policies does not meet this requirement, as the number of deterministic nature policies is infinite, and therefore, the mixed policy space is infinite-dimensional.
Instead, we show that our occupancy game is a convex semi-infinite game as defined in
Lopez and
Vercher [1986]
and given below:

Definition 22

(Convex semi-infinite game [Lopez and Vercher, 1986])
.

Given an arbitrary, possibly infinite set
T
, a convex semi-infinite game is a zero-sum game with policy sets
\Gamma
and
C
of the following types:

•

\Gamma=\{\vec{\lambda}=(\lambda_{t})_{t\in T}\mid\text{only finitely many }\lambda_{t}\neq 0,\lambda_{t}\geq 0,\text{ and }\sum_{t\in T}\lambda_{t}=1\}
.

•

C=
a nonempty closed convex set in
\mathbb{R}^{n}
with
n\in\mathbb{N}
a finite number.

And a family of convex functions with finite values
\mathcal{F}_{T}=\{F_{t}\colon\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}\mid t\in T\}
, such that the value function of the convex semi-infinite game
W\colon C\times\Gamma\to\mathbb{R}
is:

W(\vec{x},\vec{\lambda})=\sum_{t\in T}\lambda_{t}F_{t}(\vec{x})\text{, with }\vec{\lambda}\in\Gamma\text{ and }\vec{x}\in C.

Theorem 7

(Occupancy game is convex semi-infinite)
.

Given an RPOMDP
M
and horizon
K\in\mathbb{N}
, the corresponding occupancy game OG (
Definition

19
) is an convex semi-infinite game, where:

•

T
is the set of deterministic nature policies
\Theta^{det}_{0:K-1}
.

•

\Gamma
is the set of mixed nature policies
\Theta^{mix}_{0:K-1}
.

•

C
is the set of mixed agent policies
\Pi^{mix}_{0:K-1}
.

•

F_{\theta^{det}}(\vec{x})=\sum_{\pi^{det}\in\Pi^{det}_{0:K-1}}x_{\pi^{det}}\cdot V^{\pi^{det},\theta^{det}}
with
\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{det}_{0:K-1}=T
and
\vec{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}
where
n
is the finite number of deterministic agent policies
|\Pi^{det}_{0:K-1}|
.

Note that we omitted the history length indication for the policies for readability purposes.
The history lengths on which the policies are defined can be derived from the policy sets from which they are taken.
See
Table

2
in
Appendix

A
for the notation glossary.

We prove
Theorem

7
by proving several smaller lemmas, showing that the suggested mapping of the occupancy game to the convex semi-infinite game definition is correct.

Lemma

11
shows that the set of mixed agent policies
\Pi^{mix}_{0:K-1}
meets the conditions for policy set
C
of the convex semi-infinite game definition.

Lemma 11
.

\Pi^{mix}_{0:K-1}
is a nonempty closed convex set in
\mathbb{R}^{n}
with
n=|\Pi^{det}_{0:K-1}|
a finite number.

Proof.

By definition,
\Pi^{mix}_{0:K-1}=\Delta(\Pi^{det}_{0:K-1})
.
Since the set of actions
A
, the set of agent observation
Z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}}
, and the set of public observation
Z_{\circ}
are all finite and nonempty, the number of deterministic policies
|\Pi^{det}_{0:K-1}|
is finite and nonempty and less than or equal to

\sum_{t=0}^{K}(|A|\cdot|Z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet}|\cdot|Z_{\circ}|)^{t}\cdot|A|.

Let
n
be the actual number of different deterministic policies in our RPOMDP.
Then we know the set of mixed policies
\Pi^{mix}_{0:K-1}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}
with
n
a finite number.
Finally, since the set of mixed policies is the probability simplex
\Delta(\Pi^{det}_{0:K-1})=\Delta(\mathbb{R}^{n})
, we know that it is a closed and convex set.
∎

As no restrictions are given on
T
, we can take the infinite set of deterministic nature policies
\Theta^{det}_{0:K-1}
.

Lemma

12
shows that the mixed nature policies then meet the conditions for policy set
\Gamma
of the convex semi-infinite game definition.

Lemma 12
.

\Theta^{mix}_{0:K-1}
is the set of finite probability distributions over the set of deterministic nature policies
\Theta^{det}_{0:K-1}
:

\Theta^{mix}_{0:K-1}=\{\vec{\lambda}=(\lambda_{\theta^{det}})_{\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{det}_{0:K-1}}\mid\text{only finitely many }\lambda_{\theta^{det}}\neq 0,\lambda_{\theta^{det}}\geq 0,\text{ and }\sum_{\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{det}_{0:K-1}}\lambda_{\theta^{det}}=1\}.

Proof.

By definition, the set of mixed nature policies
\Theta^{mix}_{0:K-1}
is the set of probability distributions over the set of deterministic nature policies
\Theta^{det}_{0:K-1}
.
As stated in
Section

2
, we only consider finite probability distributions over infinite sets.
The set of mixed nature policies is hence also restricted to the finite probability distributions.
This means
\vec{\lambda}=\theta^{mix}\in\Theta^{mix}_{0:K-1}
with
\lambda_{\theta^{det}}=\theta^{mix}(\theta^{det})
.
∎

Recall the family of functions
F_{\theta^{det}}\colon\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}
defined on the set of deterministic nature policies
\Theta^{det}_{0:K-1}
in
Theorem

7
:

F_{\theta^{det}}(x_{\pi^{det}})=\sum_{\pi^{det}\in\Pi^{det}_{0:K-1}}x_{\pi^{det}}\cdot V^{\pi^{det},\theta^{det}}.

The next two lemmas show that this family of functions
F_{\theta^{det}}
is convex (
Lemma

13
) and all functions in the family have a finite value (
Lemma

14
).

Lemma 13
.

\forall\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{det}_{0:K-1}.\;F_{\theta^{det}}
is a convex function.

Proof.

Take arbitrary
\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{det}_{0:K-1}
,
\vec{x},\vec{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}
, and
\alpha\in[0,1]
then:

\displaystyle F_{\theta^{det}}(\alpha\cdot\vec{x}+(1-\alpha)\cdot\vec{y})

\displaystyle=\sum_{\pi^{det}\in\Pi^{det}}(\alpha\cdot\vec{x}+(1-\alpha)\cdot\vec{y})_{\pi^{det}}\cdot V^{\pi^{det},\theta^{det}}

\displaystyle=\sum_{\pi^{det}\in\Pi^{det}}(\alpha\cdot x_{\pi^{det}}+(1-\alpha)\cdot y_{\pi^{det}})\cdot V^{\pi^{det},\theta^{det}}

\displaystyle=\sum_{\pi^{det}\in\Pi^{det}}\alpha\cdot x_{\pi^{det}}\cdot V^{\pi^{det},\theta^{det}}+(1-\alpha)\cdot y_{\pi^{det}}\cdot V^{\pi^{det},\theta^{det}}

\displaystyle=\sum_{\pi^{det}\in\Pi^{det}}\bigl\{\alpha\cdot x_{\pi^{det}}\cdot V^{\pi^{det},\theta^{det}}\bigr\}+\sum_{\pi^{det}\in\Pi^{det}}\bigl\{(1-\alpha)\cdot y_{\pi^{det}}\cdot V^{\pi^{det},\theta^{det}}\bigr\}

\displaystyle=\alpha\cdot\sum_{\pi^{det}\in\Pi^{det}}\bigl\{x_{\pi^{det}}\cdot V^{\pi^{det},\theta^{det}}\bigr\}+(1-\alpha)\cdot\sum_{\pi^{det}\in\Pi^{det}}\bigl\{y_{\pi^{det}}\cdot V^{\pi^{det},\theta^{det}}\bigr\}

\displaystyle=\alpha\cdot F_{\theta^{det}}(\vec{x})+(1-\alpha)\cdot F_{\theta^{det}}(\vec{y}).

So
\forall_{\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{det}}.\;F_{\theta^{det}}
is a convex function.
∎

Lemma 14
.

Given
\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{det}
,
\vec{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}
:

F_{\theta^{det}}(\vec{x})\text{ has a finite value.}

Proof.

\forall\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{det},\forall\pi^{det}\in\Pi^{det}
the value of
V^{\pi^{det}_{i},\theta^{det}}
is finite, as it is bounded by
K\cdot(\max_{s,a\in S\times A}R(s,a))
.
Furthermore,
\vec{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}
can only take finite values.
Together, this shows that:

\forall\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{det},\forall\pi^{det}\in\Pi^{det}.\,F_{\theta^{det}}(\vec{x})\text{ has a finite value}.

∎

Finally,
Lemma

15
shows that the value function
W\colon\Pi^{mix}_{0:K-1}\times\Theta^{mix}_{0:K-1}\to\mathbb{R}
of the convex semi-infinite game constructed as in
Theorem

7
is equivalent to the value function
V\colon\Pi^{mix}_{0:K-1}\times\Theta^{mix}_{0:K-1}\to\mathbb{R}
of the occupancy game.

Lemma 15
.

The value function of the convex semi-infinite game is equivalent to the value function of the occupancy game.

\forall\pi^{mix}\in\Pi^{mix}_{0:K-1},\forall\theta^{mix}\in\Theta^{mix}_{0:K-1}.\,W(\pi^{mix},\theta^{mix})=V^{\pi^{mix},\theta^{mix}}.

Proof.

Recall the definition of the value function of a convex semi-infinite game:

W(\pi^{mix},\theta^{mix})=\sum_{\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{det}}\theta^{mix}(\theta^{det})\cdot F_{\theta^{det}}(\pi^{mix}).

By construction, the value function of our occupancy game is the same as that of our original RPOMDP.
However, as shown in
Section

G.3
, we can reason with mixed policies, giving us the following value function:

V^{\pi^{mix},\theta^{mix}}=\sum_{\pi^{det}\in\Pi^{det}}\pi^{mix}(\pi^{det})\cdot\sum_{\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{det}}\theta^{mix}(\theta^{det})\cdot V^{\pi^{det},\theta^{det}}.

Take arbitrary mixed agent and nature policies
\pi^{mix}\in\Pi^{mix}_{0:K-1},\theta^{mix}\in\Theta^{mix}_{0:K-1}
.
Then:

\displaystyle W(\pi^{mix},\theta^{mix})

\displaystyle=\sum_{\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{det}}\theta^{mix}(\theta^{det})\cdot F_{\theta^{det}}(\pi^{mix})

\displaystyle=\sum_{\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{det}}\theta^{mix}(\theta^{det})\cdot\sum_{\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{det}}\pi^{mix}(\pi^{det})\cdot V^{\pi^{det},\theta^{det}}

\displaystyle=\sum_{\pi^{det}\in\Pi^{det}}\pi^{mix}(\pi^{det})\cdot\sum_{\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{det}}\theta^{mix}(\theta^{det})\cdot V^{\pi^{det},\theta^{det}}

\displaystyle=V^{\pi^{mix},\theta^{mix}}.

∎

Lemma

15
is the final step in proving
Theorem

7
.
We conclude that our occupancy game is a convex semi-infinite game.

The final step in proving the existence of a finite horizon Nash equilibrium in our RPOMDPs follows from
[
Lopez and
Vercher, 1986
, Theorem 3.2]
, stating that in a convex semi-infinite game, if the convex functions and the convex agent policy set have no common direction of recession, then a Nash equilibrium and an optimal strategy for the agent exist.

Lemma 16
.

In the convex semi-infinite game of our occupancy game, the convex functions
F_{\theta^{det}}
with
\theta^{det}\in\Theta^{det}
and the set of mixed agent policies
\Pi^{mix}
have no common direction of recession.

Proof.

As our set of agent policies is a convex polytope in
\mathbb{R}^{n}
, it is a closed and bounded convex subset of
\mathbb{R}^{n}
.
Then, the recession cone consists only of the zero vector
Zalinescu [2002]
.
The zero vector is also trivially contained in the recession cones of the convex functions.
Therefore, we know that the convex functions and the convex agent policy set have no common direction of recession.
∎

As shown in
Lemma

16
, our occupancy game meets the condition given in
Lopez and
Vercher [1986]
.
It hence follows that a Nash equilibrium and an optimal strategy for the agent exist and that the saddle point condition holds, proving Theorem
3
.

G.5
Nature First

When reasoning with the nature first semantics, the nature policy no longer relies on the last action of the agent.
This influences the proof of the sufficient statistic as follows:

\displaystyle\text{OS}_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t}}(\langle h_{t},a_{t},u_{t},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},z_{\circ}\rangle)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\langle\sigma_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t}}(\langle h_{t},a_{t},u_{t},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},z_{\circ}\rangle),\theta_{0:t}\rangle,

where:

\displaystyle\theta_{0:t}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\langle\theta_{0:t-1},\theta_{t}\rangle.

\displaystyle\sigma_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t}}(\langle h_{t},a_{t},u_{t},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},z_{\circ}\rangle)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\Pr(h_{t},a_{t},u_{t},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},z_{\circ}\mid\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t})

\displaystyle=\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{n}}}\sum_{s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{n}}}\Pr(z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},z_{\circ}\mid s^{\prime})\Pr(s^{\prime}\mid a_{t},u_{t},s)\Pr(h_{t},a_{t},u_{t},s\mid\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t})

\displaystyle=\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{n}}}\sum_{s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{n}}}\Pr(z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},z_{\circ}\mid s^{\prime})\Pr(s^{\prime}\mid a_{t},u_{t},s)\Pr(u_{t}\mid h_{t},a_{t},s,\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t})\Pr(h_{t},a_{t},s\mid\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t}).

The chance of a nature action only depends on nature’s policy at time
t
and the history:

\displaystyle=\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{n}}}\sum_{s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{n}}}\Pr(z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},z_{\circ}\mid s^{\prime})\Pr(s^{\prime}\mid a_{t},u_{t},s)\Pr(u_{t}\mid h_{t},\theta_{t})\Pr(h_{t},a_{t},s\mid\pi_{0:t},\theta_{0:t})

\displaystyle=\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{n}}}\sum_{s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{n}}}\Pr(z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},z_{\circ}\mid s^{\prime})\Pr(s^{\prime}\mid a_{t},u_{t},s)\Pr(u_{t}\mid h_{t},a_{t},\theta_{t})\Pr(a_{t}\mid h_{t},\pi_{t})\Pr(s\mid h_{t})\Pr(h_{t}\mid\pi_{0:t-1},\theta_{0:t-1})

\displaystyle=\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{n}}}\sum_{s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{n}}}\mathcal{O}^{\mathfrak{a}}(s^{\prime},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}},z_{\circ},)\mathcal{O}^{\mathfrak{n}}(s^{\prime},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},z_{\circ})\mathcal{T}^{\mathfrak{a}}(\mathcal{T}^{\mathfrak{n}}(s,u_{t}),a_{t},s^{\prime})\theta_{t}(h^{\mathfrak{n}}_{t},u_{t})\pi_{t}(h^{\mathfrak{a}}_{t},a_{t})b(s,h_{t})\sigma_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t-1}}(h_{t}).

We can hence still compute the successor occupancy state using only the previous occupancy state
\text{OS}_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t-1}}=\langle\sigma_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t-1}},\theta_{0:t-1}\rangle
and policies
\pi_{t},\theta_{t}
at time
t
.
The expected reward proof requires no modifications.

We define the nature first OG as follows:

Definition 23

(OG)
.

Given a POSG as defined in
Definition

18

\langle\mathcal{S^{\mathfrak{a}},S^{\mathfrak{n}},A^{\mathfrak{a}},A^{\mathfrak{n}},T,R,Z^{\mathfrak{a}},Z^{\mathfrak{n}},O^{\mathfrak{a}},O^{\mathfrak{n}}}\rangle
, and a horizon
K\in\mathbb{N}
, we define the OG as a tuple
(\mathsf{S}^{\mathfrak{a}},\mathsf{S}^{\mathfrak{n}},\mathsf{A}^{\mathfrak{a}},\mathsf{A}^{\mathfrak{n}},\mathsf{T},\mathsf{R})
where the sets of states and actions are defined as follows:

\mathsf{S}^{\mathfrak{a}}=\bigcup_{t=0}^{K-1}(\bigcup_{\pi_{0:t}\in\Pi_{0:t}}\bigcup_{\theta_{0:t}\in\Theta_{0:t}}\text{OS}_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t}}\times\Theta_{t+1})
is the infinite set of agent states, and
\mathsf{S}^{\mathfrak{n}}=\bigcup_{t=0}^{K-1}\bigcup_{\pi_{0:t}\in\Pi_{0:t}}\bigcup_{\theta_{0:t}\in\Theta_{0:t}}\text{OS}_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t}}
the infinite set of nature states;

\mathsf{A}^{\mathfrak{a}}=\bigcup_{t=0}^{K-1}\Pi_{t}
is the infinite set of agent actions, and
\mathsf{A}^{\mathfrak{n}}=\bigcup_{t=0}^{K-1}\Theta_{t}
the infinite set of nature actions;
The transition and reward functions are then defined as:

•

\mathsf{T}=\mathsf{T}^{\mathfrak{a}}\cup\mathsf{T}^{\mathfrak{n}}
, the transition function, where:

–

\mathsf{T}^{\mathfrak{a}}\colon\mathsf{S}^{\mathfrak{a}}\times\mathsf{A}^{\mathfrak{a}}\hookrightarrow\mathsf{S}^{\mathfrak{n}}
the agent’s transition function.

–

\mathsf{T}^{\mathfrak{n}}\colon\mathsf{S}^{\mathfrak{n}}\times\mathsf{A}^{\mathfrak{n}}\hookrightarrow\mathsf{S}^{\mathfrak{a}}
nature’s transition function.

•

\mathsf{R}\colon\mathsf{S}^{\mathfrak{a}}\times\mathsf{A}^{\mathfrak{a}}\to\mathbb{R}
the reward function.

Where:

•

\mathsf{R}(\langle\sigma_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t}},\theta_{0:t}\rangle,\pi_{t+1})=\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{a}}}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{a}}}\Bigl\{\mathcal{R}(s,a)\cdot\sum_{h_{t+1}\in H_{t+1}(\theta_{0:t})}\bigl\{\pi_{t+1}(h_{t+1},a)b(s,h_{t+1})\sigma_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t}}(h_{t+1})\bigr\}\Bigr\}
.

•

\mathsf{T^{\mathfrak{n}}}(\langle\sigma_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t}},\theta_{0:t}\rangle,\theta_{t+1})=\langle\langle\sigma_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t}},\theta_{0:t}\rangle,\theta_{t+1}\rangle
.

•

\mathsf{T^{\mathfrak{a}}}(\langle\langle\sigma_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t}},\theta_{0:t}\rangle,\theta_{t+1}\rangle,\pi_{t+1})=\langle\sigma_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t+1}},\theta_{0:t+1}\rangle
, where:

–

\theta_{0:t+1}=\theta_{0:t}\oplus\theta_{t+1}
.

–

\forall h_{t+1}\in H_{t+1}(\theta_{0:t}),\forall a\in\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{a}},\forall u\in\mathcal{A}^{\mathfrak{n}},\forall z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\in Z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}}\times Z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}}\times Z_{\circ},\sigma_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t+1}}(\langle h_{t+1},a,u,z^{\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet},z^{\mathfrak{n}}_{\bullet},z_{\circ}\rangle)=

\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{n}}}\sum_{s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}^{\mathfrak{n}}}\mathcal{O}^{\mathfrak{a}}(s^{\prime},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{a}},z_{\circ},)\mathcal{O}^{\mathfrak{n}}(s^{\prime},z_{\bullet}^{\mathfrak{n}},z_{\circ})\mathcal{T}^{\mathfrak{a}}(\mathcal{T}^{\mathfrak{n}}(s,u_{t}),a_{t},s^{\prime})\theta_{t}(h^{\mathfrak{n}}_{t},u_{t})\pi_{t}(h^{\mathfrak{a}}_{t},a_{t})b(s,h_{t})\sigma_{\{\pi,\theta\}_{0:t-1}}(h_{t}).

Where
b(s,h_{t})
is the belief computed by
t
belief updates given the joint history
h_{t}
.
Where
H_{t}(\theta_{0:t-1})\subset H_{t}
is the subset with
u_{i}\in\bm{U}
determined by
\theta_{i}
given the history
h^{\mathfrak{n}}_{0:i-1}
and action
a
. This is a finite subset of the infinite set of possible joint histories.

To show that for every stochastic policy there exists a mixed policy that behaves equivalently and vice versa in the nature first setting, the proofs follow the same steps as in
Section

G.3
for the agent first policies.
The only required changes are to remove the agent action input for the nature policies and the corresponding
\forall a\in A
.

The nature first OG still meets all requirements for having an optimal value, which can be shown by following the same proof steps as for the agent first OG in
Section

G.4
.
